This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a sequence of constrained optimization problems that can be iteratively refined. Our method, AskewSGD, is an efficient first-order stochastic approach designed to solve each optimization subproblem. Unlike conventional algorithms, AskewSGD circumvents computationally intensive projections and does not require smoothing the objective function, thus enabling a more direct approach to constrained optimization. Our technique enables a more flexible error metric and allows for a broader class of quantized neural network training. AskewSGD's performance is showcased on ImageNet using BNNs trained with the cross-entropy loss and top-1 accuracy, where it achieves comparable results with existing methods while demonstrating improvements in speed.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve agile and adaptable robotics capabilities. These robots are designed with internal and external stability in mind, allowing their cores to resist external forces and facilitate precise external interactions. Research in this area has made significant progress in the development of open-loop and closed-loop control systems, capable of generating motion and adapting to various environments. However, many challenges still lie within the control of multi-body continuum robots, particularly in their interaction with the surroundings. To bridge this knowledge gap, this paper presents an innovative approach to controlling non-reversible continuum robots with multiple segments, capable of shifting the center of mass internally while adapting to external external forces and deformations through real-time feedback and modeling of the robot's dynamics and geometry. Evaluations were conducted using the proposed method on a 5-segment robot with a movable center of mass and external forces. These tests showed the method could accurately predict and respond to the robot's behavior and interactions, demonstrating a high value for real-time feedback control applications. The method's assumptions and potential limitations were also identified, paving the way for further research in this field.

The Jacobi group, denoted as G^J_1(ℝ), is a geometrically significant hybrid of the special linear group, Heisenberg group, and Dirac clasper group all combined. While well-known for its applications in physics, thermodynamics, and number theory, we focus specifically on real Jacobi movements G^J_1(ℝ) and establish a dual parameterization. Through initial group operations, this real Jacobi group forms a solvable Lie group, thus providing an opportunity to tackle central issues like abelian covers and the extended cohomology theory developed by Borel, Eberhard, and others. A new theorem arises, describing the second cohomology space of the fundamental abelian cover of the Jacobi group, which is a highly intrinsic generalization of the Baer abelian extension of the SL(2,ℝ) group. Furthermore, this realization offers the potential for far-reaching applications in geometry, the theory of Lie groups, and their respective Lie algebras.

Verifying facts using structured data can be challenging, necessitating a model's
understanding of both language and symbolic computations involving data in
tables. Despite pre-trained language models excelling in confirming simple facts,
they struggle with fact verification involving structured data requiring multiple
interrelated calculations. This difficulty prompted an investigation into
whether these models can learn in a gradual manner, starting from facts involving
less complex computations, as younger models tend to perform better on those.
An icon-based method was developed where a icon-based language, resembling math
symbols, simplifies the task and an icon-based transformer was proposed as a
prototype. An evaluation was conducted using the FactCheckNet dataset, which
compares the performance of - a, a variant with minimal icon usage, a, a variant
without icons, and a plus the effectiveness of icon usage. Results revealed that
adding icons significantly improved the performance of as much as 21, and its
underlying model as much as 26.

The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised approaches, however, current advancements are primarily based on labelled data, leading to increased control, flexibility, and stability in the generated images. Notably, these supervised methods require substantial amounts of annotated data, posing a major challenge for various domains. Our research aims to bridge the gap between the versatility of supervised approaches and the ability of unsupervised methods to learn from minimal to no labelled data. To achieve this, we introduce a new framework that combines two separate models, one trained on labelled data and the other on unlabelled data, into a single multi-modal latent space. This approach enables the integration of additional semantic information into the learned representation, ultimately facilitating the generation of high-quality, semantically-controlled synthetic images with both unconditional and conditioned variants. Our contributions are outlined as follows: (1) We present a new framework for synthetic image generation that leverages two models with different learning objectives, one trained on labelled data and the other on unlabelled data. (2) We demonstrate that this approach allows for the incorporation of annotated semantics into the learned representation, (3) We showcase high-quality, synthetic images generated with various conditions, including one that utilises a pre-trained semantic segmentation model, and (4) We perform an in-depth ablation study to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on multiple datasets, with additional findings detailed in our appended supplementary material.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. Researchers have developed methods like Markov Chain Monte Carlo derivatives for complex, high-dimensional problems. A study examined ten different algorithms, incorporating techniques like cutting Gaussian ridges, shifting and multiplying samples, along with dual and triple pruning, all aimed at efficiently selecting these distinctive prior samples. The research found that certain algorithms consistently outperformed others and proved particularly robust when dealing with varying numbers of dimensions, ranging from 1 to 100. Moreover, it was discovered that no single algorithm excelled in all scenarios, highlighting the importance of evaluating algorithms carefully depending on the specific task at hand.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any three points' labels allows us to deduce the direct distance between any two of them, excluding the third. This study focuses on fault-tolerant distance labelling in graphs that feature low diameter (at most $D$) and few vertices ($n$), with a constant label length resulting, which is crucial for applications involving wireless sensors in rugged terrain. We prove that it's possible to create these labels in a time complexity of $O(n \log n)$ and space complexity of $O(n)$ by using a data structure that helps us determine the second-highest height in a collection of segments - a problem resembling the $k$-center clustering problem. We also show that similar label assignment techniques can be applied to trees and other shared networks, with further applications extending to scheduling in parallel machines and designing efficient packet routing systems. Additionally, we explore the combinatorial aspects of this problem and derive both upper and lower bounds for the feasible label lengths and other related constraints. We implement these findings in an algorithm that deterministically assigns labels with a specific length in a particular graph structure - a product graph with layered trees ($S(D, n)$). Notably, this algorithm achieves a label length result that matches our main theoretical findings and offers a polynomial time complexity. In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a low-density, weakly interacting Bose gas, addressing an open mathematical issue from the 1980s. Our approach involves using the Dyson series to simplify the non-stationary Schrödinger operator, and we discover that the two-particle correlation function oscillates at distinct frequencies represented by the imaginary components of the Liouvillian gap and Green's function eigenvalues. Notably, these frequencies remain evident even in a nonlinear regime and strongly depend on the initial quantum state of the system. Frequency spectra can be categorized into three types and we calculate the corresponding oscillation periods using an asymptotic analysis of the Liouvillian spectrum. Our findings will be valuable for developing new methods for measuring Bose gas temperature and frequency spectra using time-resolved spectroscopy.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\lambda$, defined within a bounded $\mathbb{R}^2$ domain $\Omega$ and satisfying specific smoothness and boundedness conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the weak solution in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ for the Dirichlet problem, where $2<p<\infty$, assuming that the equation also includes source and flux terms. Similar results are obtained for the corresponding dual problem under analogous conditions.

To ensure that medical imaging models produce accurate results, it is crucial to implement out-of-distribution detection capabilities. There are instances where a model may generate unrealistic images, and being able to identify such instances is essential. Our research focuses on detecting unrealistically distorted images generated by these models. Our method employs a multi-task approach on pre-trained UNet models to achieve this. By extending the pre-trained UNet with detection capabilities, our approach can effectively identify distorted images. Using the CheXpert model as an example, our approach achieved a high Area Under the ROC Curve score of 0.954 when testing for highly abnormal images. Similarly, our approach achieved a high Area Under the ROC Curve score of 0.920 when testing for moderately abnormal images. Our approach also effectively detected unrealistically distorted images, achieving a high F1 score of 0.918. Our approach can be used as a post-processing step to identify and remove unrealistic images generated by models, thus ensuring that the results are reliable.

Quantum systems driven periodically experience heat build-up due to resonant excitations, typically leading to a random thermal state. In contrast, a system that is both driven and in contact with a heat bath will instead converge towards a distinct, out-of-balance stable condition. Our study shows that weak, persistent interference within the system's excitations can interrupt this random thermal pattern and cause a sudden change in its behavior. This phenomenon occurs for any type of heat bath and can be observed in driven, classically unstable systems such as the one-sided hard disk oscillator as well as in driven, quantum mechanical systems such as the kicked top when including quantum fluctuations.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ of the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in an open convex domain with a nonnegative, bounded right-hand side, along with specific boundary data. A key finding relates Alexandrov's maximum principle, specifically its equivalence to H\"older continuity, for convex functions with zero boundary data. Furthermore, it has been proven that convex $\alpha$-H\"older continuous functions fall into $W^{1,p}$ for $p<1/(1{-}\alpha)$. Crucially, this research establishes the H\"older continuity of the convex solution $u$ under specific boundary data, with sharp bounds for the exponent derived through a method involving a bounding Hessian determinant on an n-dimensional cylinder.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant undertaking. We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicking mechanisms. A comprehensive statistical analysis framework is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of these devices, with a specific example being a single two-level atom driven coherently and monitored via photodetection, representing an extreme instance of a non-repeating clock. Using Quantum Jump Monte Carlo simulations and the photon counting waiting time distribution will independently validate the main findings.

This research accomplishes two objectives: implementing a Fog computing system alongside a Software Defined Network and then refining it with application of Reinforcement Learning techniques. The main focus lies in optimizing the Fog-SDN integration through two principal objectives - enhancing Quality of Service (QoS) and energy consumption (ENP) - by using RL, which initially requires learning the best action to take in each situation from the current state. The primary challenge here lies in the diverse action sets taken by central controllers in both Fog-SDN and SDN systems. To address this, the paper presents two RL algorithms for the two networks: the first algorithm integrates observed values from RL, action sets from the central controller, and action values from the controller to find the optimal value approximation. The second algorithm extends the first with a more comprehensive observation set, including link loads, Fog computing resource loads, and encoding rates, which are all crucial for RL to determine the best action to take in each situation. The results from the simulations conducted validate the efficiency of the two algorithms against existing models.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse set of loss functions, we've isolated the key aspects that dictate how these functions work. Our research is a comprehensive examination of five essential properties of pair-wise loss functions, and we've demonstrated how these properties dictate the behavior of these functions.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that a specific network, comprising a single Riemann surface's conformal data, can serve as a fundamental, universal building block for constructing networks capable of withstanding multiple, diverse distortions. This discovery enables the creation of new, versatile quantum codes leveraging a variety of tensors associated with Poincaré metrics, thereby offering a richer understanding of the potential structure and diversity of network designs.

Our study of magnetized radio filaments at the center of the galaxy utilizes MeerKAT data by examining the distances between groups of these filaments. A sample of 43 groupings containing 174 radio filaments was studied and their shapes were analyzed. Many grouped filaments were found to resemble harp strings or comets with looped tails, in contrast to the mostly straight filaments that lie perpendicular to the galactic plane. We also observed filaments that split into two at a single point, possibly due to the movement of plasma through the filaments. Changes in the spectral index, brightness, and curvature of the filaments along their length indicate that they are constantly changing on a 100,000-1,000,000 year time scale. We determined that parallel filaments in the same group have a mean distance of approximately 16 inches. By modeling, we propose that all filaments in a group lie within the same plane and the groupings themselves are evenly dispersed throughout three-dimensional space. We suggest that one potential origin for the filament pattern is due to the cooling of a rapidly expanding plasma after a series of energy releases that create shockwaves in the magnetic field, causing the plasma to accumulate along curved surfaces. Alternatively, we propose that the filament pattern is caused by the magnetic field's spiral pattern structure.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems using load representation. The system is modeled with load active and reactive power responses in relation to voltage magnitude, and the active and reactive power demands are aggregated and represented as smart meters. The load response model and system resistance, inductance, and capacitance are used to formulate the system model. The large-scale system model is then simplified into a smaller dimension system and the optimal voltage profile for each CVR step is determined through a robust optimization method with robust control droops and generation real power adjustments. The method does not require communication between devices and allows for simultaneous design of CVR and recovery responses, but does not account for emerging challenges such as electric vehicle integration. The method is evaluated on a real unbalanced test system and the results are compared with previous studies, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon both the time and arm choice. While delayed settings with time-dependent delays have been thoroughly studied, considering arm-dependent delays is more reflective of real-world applications, but raises additional technical obstacles. In the experts scenario with complete knowledge, we create an algorithm achieving a first-order regret bound, highlighting the relationship between delays and losses. This algorithm also results in a first-order regret bound for bandits, given knowledge of missing losses. For the more challenging setting of unknown losses and missing delays, we derive a regret bound using a combination of the Tsukano et al. approach for delay-only bandits and a technique from Auer et al. for expert settings. Our method yields a log(T) factor, indicating that knowing either delays or loss values significantly reduces the difficulty of the problem.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can inadvertently limit the diversity of words used, even if it means generating sentences that are less accurate by replacing essential words with less relevant alternatives. To better understand how diversity is handled in dialogue-based systems, we designed a simple test and found that reinforcement learning, a method used to improve task performance, can have the opposite effect, reducing diversity while attempting to improve dialogue ratings. To counter this effect, we developed an approach that rewards the use of less common words to generate more diverse and natural-sounding dialogue. Our approach was tested using a simulated dialogue system and found to successfully increase dialogue diversity while maintaining its accuracy. The details of our approach can be accessed at https://github.com/google/dialect.

Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened doors for in-depth numerical analyses of QCD's non-perturbative features, exemplified in the initial studies by Michael Creutz. Subsequently, investigations into the QCD phase diagram and the thermodynamics of hot, dense strong-interaction matter gained significant momentum. In this concise review, some key outcomes from over four decades of lattice QCD research on QCD thermodynamics are compiled.

A type of Gaussian process regression that accounts for the variability in data points, called heteroscedastic Gaussian process regression, is utilized to develop predictive models for the specific loads an offshore wind turbine will experience, based on its operational conditions. This study examines and compares the effectiveness of two methods for estimating variability from limited datasets, involving simulated and real load response data from turbines, showing that these methods can accurately represent and predict the variability of the data. However, when applying these methods to real datasets, which often have data points with extreme values due to censoring, significant issues arise regarding the estimated covariance matrices and the predictions made. Nevertheless, the proposed heteroscedastic models still demonstrate the ability to outperform traditional constant-variance models in predicting the specified loads.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining and natural language processing techniques, we examine public sentiment and topic discussions following the earthquake. Our approach utilized LDA for topic modeling and BERT for sentiment analysis. Results show users shared supportive messages and engaged with relief efforts, expressing their desire to have their concerns heard by authorities. The implemented methodology demonstrated success, and future directions for related studies are also outlined.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we decompose the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ as semidirect products of finitely generated abelian groups, and we identify which invertible matrices can be extended into automorphisms of $\Gamma_{n,c}$.

A new technique has been developed to process time-resolved data from ultra-fast events, which generates a three-dimensional vector field representing the source of emission. This approach, developed for analyzing data from ultra-fast events, can generate a three-dimensional vector field describing how the source of emission changes over time. A key advancement in this method is the ability to maintain the continuity of radiation patterns in the past and future, which is not possible with other techniques. Additionally, the new technique can maintain continuity beyond just the speed of light, allowing for the simulation of complex scenarios. A test was conducted using this method to recreate the November 9th 2006 Minas Gerais mini-flare from the Solar Dynamic Observatory, which showed good results. A key discovery was that the early stages of the flare radiated backwards towards the sun before rapidly increasing and shooting forwards, with the event accelerating very quickly. Two possible explanations for this behavior are that the flare event compressed the magnetic fields in a specific shape or that it was caused by the movement of plasma ions. Further research is needed to see if the new technique will yield new insights into other flare events.

This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented vehicle data collected in downtown Indianapolis over the course
of 68 driving sessions with various drivers. Each session lasted approximately
20 to 40 minutes. Our primary aim in creating this dataset is to supply the
research community with realistic driving scenarios encompassing diverse
trajectories and driving behaviors. SceNDD features a comprehensive set of data,
including the ego-vehicle's waypoints, velocity, and yaw angle, as well as
similar metrics for non-ego actors. Additionally, we allow users to customize
existing scenarios by introducing additional elements, such as actors, sensors,
lanes, roads, and obstacles. A Joint Probabilistic Data Association tracker was
utilized to identify non-ego vehicles. We present some preliminary outcomes of
the dataset, alongside potential applications, and anticipate the SceNDD to
facilitate various future research initiatives. The dataset can be accessed via
our project website at https://scebdd22.github.io.

In connection with the information paradox problem, theories such as BCFT and ICFT are gaining attention. As a contribution to this topic, we have developed an approach to reflected entropy in the context of BCFT/ICFT. Starting with BCFT, we define left-right reflected entropy and establish its dual description using AdS/BCFT, specifically through the entanglement wedge cross section area. Additionally, we have worked out how to calculate reflected entropy in ICFT. With these tools, we are able to reveal a universal behavior of the Markov gap in specific situations. Furthermore, our work has helped to clarify the holographic representation of boundary primary correlation functions via this left-right reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross section duality.

Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has intensified due to their potential for controlling the communication environment and combating multi-path interference (MPI). The limited scope of existing models, which rely on approximate methods, linearization, or Monte Carlo simulations, motivates us to develop a probability distribution function (PDF) of the received signal for RIS-OFDM systems using the Fourier series (FS) approach. Firstly, we will derive the joint PDF of the received signal's real and imaginary components. Then, we will leverage the real and imaginary components' independence to construct separate FS-based PDFs for each. Ultimately, we will combine the real and imaginary component PDFs to achieve the overall joint PDF. The accuracy of our proposed FS method will be validated through a comparison with Monte Carlo simulations, following which we will use it to estimate the bit error rate (BER) relying solely on the received signal's PDF. The results demonstrate that our FS method outperforms the existing maximum likelihood (ML) maximum a posteroir (MAP) approach, achieving comparable performance with reduced computational demands.

We are investigating a type of equality related to the work exerted on a system being measured, using an energy meter, in a quantum thermally active process. We've established that this equality holds true for a particular type of meter with the highest resolution that only measures energy, and does so with complete accuracy. We've found that the coherent states of the meter, which are aligned with the system's thermal states at a given temperature, minimize the error in measuring the work done when the system is in thermal equilibrium. Importantly, our findings also reveal how performing such a measurement impacts the coherent driving force behind a system in thermal equilibrium and also influences the system's entropy. We've also explored the broader implications of our results.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove the formality of the deformation theory for instantons and real G2-manifolds with bounded geometry. Additionally, we apply these results to the case of 7-dimensional sphere spaces with an SU(3)-invariant almost G2-strucutre.

The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and socio-economic disruption, with the rapid proliferation of the virus having far-reaching effects worldwide. As part of the effort to combat this crisis, contact tracing technology, known for its success in other outbreaks, has been widely adopted.  However, this technology poses significant concerns regarding user data security, as it entails data collection and analysis that can potentially reveal an individual's identity, location, and behavior. The implications of this are especially dire when considering large-scale government surveillance in countries with restrictive policies.  Despite national laws protecting user data, questions still persist regarding the safeguarding of individual privacy in contact tracing systems.  This study assesses the inherent privacy features of contact tracing COVID-19 apps with specific emphasis on Brazil's national Coronav′irus-SUS app due to Brazil's severe impact from the virus.  Two critical methods will be employed for evaluation: physical data analysis and functional testing.  The former examines the potential for physical data to identify users while the latter delves into the functionality of the app.  Regarding Coronav′irus-SUS, our findings reveal that this app possesses weak safeguards protecting user data.  Given this, a proposed solution has been devised to enhance the app's security through the implementation of an inversion table to diffuse users' data and a password manager to facilitate secure account access.  The proposed method will be applied to Coronav′irus-S

The central nervous system's underlying physiological processes that drive conscious experiences have long been the focal point of research in cognitive neuroscience. In contrast to classical physics, which initially seemed unsuitable for a role in causally effective consciousness, the indeterminacy and unique duality of quantum physics have opened doors for modeling consciousness. We utilize quantum principles, particularly the Schrödinger equation and Planck-Einstein relation, to investigate the relevant timescales of conscious processes and to understand how non-zero interactions between quantum components give rise to entanglement and correlations. We demonstrate, employing a measure of entanglement based on Schmidt decomposition, that interactions between quantum subsystems can indeed generate both entanglement and separable states, which in turn enable potential applications in artificial intelligence and conscious states of awareness. We explore the role of quantum coherence, the associated phenomena of wave-function collapse, and the employed measure of entanglement in contexts of quantum cognition and conscious experience. We also delve into the expectations surrounding future contributions from quantum-inspired and quantum-plastic approaches to artificial intelligence, as well as ongoing research into the relevant timescales of conscious processes.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A cluster of young compact asteroids connected to 39991 Iochroma undergoes a dynamics analysis in this study. Our findings show the Iochroma family's location within two adjacent three-body resonance zones: 3J-1M-3 and 5J-1M-3, where we establish that Xingming and N native asteroids are confined to the former and Xingming specifically orbits within it. Moreover, the paper calculates the orbital positions of previously discovered asteroids within five years and Xingming's precise orbital elements are determined using eccentricity and precession adjustments. In a comparative analysis, the paper's findings confirm the presence of the 3J-1M-3 resonance within the Iochroma family and its key role in stabilizing Xingming's and other compact asteroid orbits. To this end, the study presents two novel stationary points around Jupiter: one situated at 3J-1M-3 and the other at 5J-1M-3, with their respective second-order magnitudes evaluated. In particular, the study's calculations for the 3J-1M-3 resonance yield a minimum value of $|U_{2,J,3J-1M3}|$, ranging between 0.0008 and 0.0011, for Xingming's orbital parameters. Building upon Ramanujan's well-known formula for odd zeta values, we establish a related expression using the Hurwitz zeta function. We introduce a novel integral kernel that relates to the Hurwitz zeta function and serves as an extension of the integral kernel linked to Ramanujan's identity. Additionally, we deduce various infinite families of identities comparable to Ramanujan's formula.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition, specifically a sum of T-equivariant cohomologies of complex projective spaces derived from irreducible representations of T. Furthermore, the calculated cohomology is shown to be isomorphic to the product of the 1|2-dimensional T^2-equivariant elliptic cohomology of the point, and the ordinary cohomology of the complex projective space P(V) under the isomorphism between T and U(1), thereby demonstrating a connection with T^2-equivariant cohomology of the point P(T).

Recent uses of machine learning in algebraic geometry and physics are explored,  
revealing how problems in this field can be easily translated into tensor mapping,  
a concept suitable for supervised learning, as well as offering a chance to use unsupervised  
methods to analyze geometrical data. A primary aspect of this project involves understanding  
how to use geometry within machine learning, as well as how artificial intelligence can be applied  
to advance mathematical research. This discussion is featured as a chapter within the book,  
Machine learning and Algebraic Geometry, edited by A. Kasprzyk.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of the angular distributions in $J/\psi$ production through $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta, \gamma$ and the $\chi_{c0}, \chi_{c1}$ systems produced in $e^{+}+e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta, \gamma$ or $\mu^{+} \mu^{-}$. In contrast, the calculated coefficients are similar to those obtained through $\psi'(2S)$ decay. Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, both groups used Strong PINs, but differed in their method of selection. Enthusiasts deliberately chose Strong PINs, whereas casual users relied on random numbers knowing they provided additional security. Despite both groups using PINs, we discovered that casual users were more likely to report issues with PINs, indicating a need for improved education about PINs and their functionality.

This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to efficiently and precisely evaluate the integrals of products involving the solar irradiance function, as defined by ASTM standards, and user-defined smooth functions. The method's ability to produce highly accurate results with a minimal number of evaluations makes it particularly suitable for functions that are smooth in nature. While the solar irradiance function does exhibit periodic variability, this smoothness characteristic makes the solar irradiance an ideal candidate for evaluation using the described quadrature rules. However, when dealing with functions that are not smooth, such as those exhibiting periodic or non-periodic behavior, more sophisticated quadrature rules would be required. The example presented in this study calculates the energy equivalent of 1 kW-h of solar power on a horizontal surface located at an elevation angle of 35 degrees. Using 11 evaluations, this method achieves an estimated accuracy of less than 0.00001 kW-h, which indicates a high degree of precision.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation holds significant value in developing training algorithms for deep networks. However, current methods based on automatic differentiation and Kronecker-factored block diagonal approximations disregard noise in mini-batch datasets. Our new model, ViViT, capitalizes on the low-rank structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton approximation without introducing additional simplifications, enabling efficient computation of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and per-sample directional derivatives. This allows ViViT to achieve a balance between computational cost and accuracy, making it scalable for determining eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and derivatives with a time complexity of O(N^2) and a memory cost of O(N), where N represents the number of samples within a mini-batch. Our experimental findings demonstrate that ViViT offers improved performance, reduced noise, and lower training costs compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, including an experimentally verified reduction in the rank of the Hessian.

Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender category. Our research reveals that certain gender-based characteristics are preserved in statistical models of languages, including those created for German. We demonstrate that words of the same gender from the German Wörterbuch were more closely related in machine learning models than words of different genders, regardless of their semantic meaning. Notably, this gender-based distinction was also observed in a translation application, where German to English translated words tended to maintain similarities based on gender. Our findings suggest that languages influencing German may have imparted this gender-based distinction to German, which in turn affected the results of German-Chinese machine translation. Interestingly, a German-Chinese model trained solely with German data still revealed gender-based similarities, which persisted even when the input data did not directly involve gender. We discovered that the German representation of inanimate nouns, which do not naturally lend themselves to gender-based characteristics, was skewed towards feminine forms, suggesting a representation bias towards these forms. Moreover, removing bias from the German representation using a machine learning model resulted in it more closely resembling its English counterpart.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, specifically focusing on groups such as Z, Z^n, and GL(n, Z). We define and study a concept of stiffness for stationary probabilities and investigate how it relates to various aspects of these groups. Meanwhile, we describe and analyze a class of stationary probabilities associated with dual measures, confirming a previous conjecture in this area. Additionally, we derive and understand a range of inequalities related to stiffness, involving a concept of hyperbolicity and a connection to conjugacy classes, as proposed in a prior work. The consequences of these findings include new insights into the scaling properties of stationary probabilities, phase transitions, and the growth patterns of these groups.

Estimating an object's pose is a crucial aspect of most visual pipelines in robots and 3D vision as a whole. This study tackles the challenge of accurately positioning new objects with no prior knowledge. This method builds on previous work in multi-object pose estimation, leveraging a trained database to identify objects and calculate their orientation. This research expands on that idea by removing the object classification requirement. This is achieved by training a network to correlate image patches with respect to the object, not with respect to the object's classification label. This allows for correlation results to be positive for any object, rather than just one. This approach also eliminates the issue of ambiguous correlations characteristic of traditional methods. This transformation significantly improves multi-object pose estimation and even extends to novel objects such as a wheelbarrow, without the need for category-specific models.

Predicting short-term traffic is a widely researched area within intelligent transportation systems. However, existing forecasting systems face significant limitations due to their reliance on real-time data. The 2022 Traffic4cast challenge at NeurIPS addressed this issue by using publicly available sparse data. Our team participated in the challenge and achieved the top two positions in the official leaderboard. We developed two network traffic prediction models: a baseline model (T4C-Baseline) that employs feature engineering and a more advanced model (T4C-EN) that leverages feature engineering and neural networks. Our approaches utilize a combination of key factors, including time of day, day of the week, location, and roadwork updates, to estimate traffic levels. Our results indicate that a well-designed forecasting model combined with well-optimized feature engineering can achieve exceptional accuracy. Additionally, we analyzed and addressed a significant issue related to traffic prediction, namely, the negative impact of large traffic data deviations on forecasting accuracy. Our research demonstrates that a well-optimized forecasting model can achieve an error reduction of 0.54 EU for mean absolute error (MAE) and 0.64 EU for mean squared error (MSE) in road traffic estimation.

This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. By leveraging these properties, it significantly simplifies the process of performing causal inference on SCM without resorting to parameter estimation. We apply VACA to causal learning from non-parametric noise models and generate novel data that are consistent with these models. Moreover, we expand the scope of VACA for use in high-energy physics to complex scenarios involving multiple related systems and verify its practical implementation in collaborative settings. The source code for this project is available on GitHub, with further details documented at vagalab.net.

State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant data rate complicates radio data analysis and necessitates costly computation. Although top-tier computing facilities exist to facilitate astronomical research, there's an urgent need to develop novel algorithms and efficient computation techniques to effectively process these vast amounts of data in real-time. Our current handling methods, including convolving every scanning pattern against the target, may not be sustainable with upcoming next-generation radio interferometers set to launch soon. To mitigate this, we propose developing specialized software or hardware-based solutions to accelerate real-time processing of LOFAR data by incorporating field-of-view constraints and leveraging hardware-based Fourier transform features, as well as incorporating the spectrum's frequency structure. Additionally, we're exploring the feasibility of incorporating ancient computing techniques, such as analog convolution engines, to simplify data processing and make ancient technologies relevant again. Our aim is to ensure that ancient technologies and computing paradigms are correctly applied and acknowledged, and to make data processing more palliative for both old and new radio telescopes.

In recent years, advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven significant growth in photonics research, leading to cutting-edge photonic systems including traditional waveguides, nanoantennas, and metasurfaces. The innovative application of AI-driven methodologies empowers the development of smart photonic devices rooted in fundamental light-matter interaction principles. Artificial intelligence and machine learning concepts are rapidly transforming the underlying physics of light, offering effective tools to investigate metaphotonics, which relies on optically-induced resonances. We now present an overview of metaphotonics, along with a concise summary of the core principles of machine learning, exemplified through its applications to metasystems and metasurfaces.

The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office has become a daunting task.  With the line between a blockbuster and a financial loss increasingly blurred, major production companies are struggling to make informed decisions about their investments.  With advancements in data analytics and the availability of more extensive datasets, there is an increased desire to develop a comprehensive understanding of the box office success factors.  A key challenge in addressing this lies in the scarcity of a large, reliable dataset that accurately represents the box office performance.  This research presents a robust extension of the IMDb dataset with an over 1.5M entries, making it the largest publicly available dataset.  Our analysis of this expanded dataset reveals new insights on the relationship between IMDb stars and a movie's global revenue, highlighting a connection between global revenue and stars.  Interestingly, this relationship indicates revenue growth accelerates at a rate of $538.  Additionally, we have found correlations between revenue and other key movie attributes such as production budget, genre, and popularity.  Our results also shed light on the influence of advertising and the effectiveness of marketing campaigns on a movie's global revenue.  In an effort to address the limitations of traditional film ranking models, we have developed a word-embedding based approach that leverages the textual content of movie reviews to create a more well-defined framework for movie evaluation.  Our results indicate that by analyzing the tone of movie reviews, we can differentiate between successful and unsuccessful

The energy shift poses a threat to the stability of the power grid's operation, 
which necessitates maintaining both voltage amplitude and frequency within 
safe limits. Research has primarily concentrated on the stability and 
frequency dynamics but largely overlooked voltage stability. This work aims to 
investigate the stability of simple networks through both linear stability and 
bulk analysis, specifically evaluating how the secondary control for frequency 
guarantees the stability of a particular power grid and also noting an observed 
stabilizing influence on voltage dynamics despite only analyzing secondary 
frequency control.

Cyber Physical Systems are transforming into cohesive units, allowing multiple systems to collaborate in achieving a complex objective, embracing a systems of systems approach. In the automotive industry, this shift is aimed at delivering advanced capabilities like smart traffic management, fleet optimization, and environmental adaptability, leading to notable ecological improvements and societal benefits. Likewise, the infrastructure sector is migrating towards a unified, highly integrated cyber-physical system, encompassing the entire value chain. Implementing Cyber-Physical Systems of Systems (CPSoS) presents several obstacles, particularly in their perceived risk profile compared to conventional systems. By breaking down the development and operation of CPSoSs into manageable components, each with well-defined interfaces, we can assure the individual risk level remains within a defined safety margin. In this paper, we concentrate on a system of systems approach in the infrastructure and automotive domains where a decoupling mechanism allows for independent development and operation of CPSoSs. Using a system decomposition technique, we assess the risk of each subsystem, ensuring the overall risk of the system does not exceed a defined safety threshold. Additionally, we outline a generic framework for management and reconfiguration based on tested risk assessment methods, promoting the system of systems approach.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets, allowing them to distinguish between competing emission models. This research employs a novel Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES to simulate polarized scattering signatures associated with a Compton process that is expected to produce an UV/X-ray excess in blazar spectra. Preliminary model results indicate that polarized scattering can significantly impact blazar spectra, potentially manifesting as an increase in linear polarization in the UV band and a distinct 'X-shaped' pattern in the SX band. Furthermore, this phenomenon shows compatibility with observed polarization patterns in several blazars, including AO 0235+164, 3C 279, and 3C 454.3.

In our study of intricate multi-dimensional environments, also known as complex landscapes, we explored their categorization based on distinct saddle types, which proves relatively straightforward. Conversely, it's the fluctuation patterns of stable points, which emerge from these environments, that pose a more critical examination. Through an in-depth analysis, we demonstrated the stationary points' stability is resonant with their topology and classification, depending on whether they reside in a smooth or irregular region. Notably, we observed that even though the characteristics of unstable points are diverse, the points themselves can only exist in two distinct forms, which are, namely the Star and Collapsible types. Furthermore, we found that the points exhibiting these two types possess distinct representative graphs and are characterized by different quantities of positive eigenvalues. Additionally, we observed that the points exhibiting these two types possess distinct representative graphs and are characterized by different quantities of positive eigenvalues. It is also worth noting that an unconventional relationship exists between the 'Star' and 'Collapsible' types, which, when viewed from a different perspective, can be considered as being mutually exclusive.

To develop optimal methods for identifying identical pure states with perfect accuracy using limited resources, we investigate effective strategies for an experiment involving multiple repetitions.  Initially, a state is chosen and, following each iteration, a decision is made whether to repeat the current state or switch to a new state.  This decision can be based on the analysis of data collected up to the current point.  Traditionally, this problem is approached by assigning probabilities to different state samples based on how likely they are to be correct, then using the optimal strategy by simulating the process many times.  In this work, we present a more efficient method that provides an exact analysis which leads to the same decision-making processes in all simulations.  A key feature of the exact method is a threshold for each state sample, beyond which it is likely that state switching will occur.  This parameter is calculated based on the relative probabilities of correct samples to the incorrect samples.  Several different models have been used to investigate how different models evolve over time, with results indicating the benefits of analyzing data online.  It has also been found that certain models with weak discrimination capabilities can still identify identical pure states with perfect accuracy by analyzing certain properties, such as correlations, which only come into play after many repetitions.  This allows for the effective use of resources, such as experiments involving ultra-cold atoms, where state switching may incur significant costs.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Baryons are generated through a process that is straightforward to understand, which involves a QCD string breaking up into causally linked parts. A simplified model, representing a QCD flux tube with properties tied to the mass spectrum of light mesons, can replicate the masses of light baryons.

Research found that the temporal variations of this speed, known as temporal spatial correlation functions, exhibit a semi-annual pattern tied to the sun's magnetic fields, a phenomenon previously observed in the 1990s but thought to be a temporary anomaly. Researchers from the NANOGrav, Parkes, European, and International Pulsar Timing Array Collaborations have discovered a significant signal of stochastic gravitational radiation originating from the Universe, which cannot be accounted for by the conventional predictions related to the gravitational wave background produced during the early Universe. Conversely, the radiation generated by the early Universe's massless neutrinos matches the observed signal strength, while the Universe's early phase transition may also contribute to the observed signal. Consequently, the discovered signal may not solely originate from the gravitational wave background. Moreover, the observed signal strength is consistent with the Universe's early phase transition occurring at a certain energy threshold. Additionally, the observed signal may provide insights into the properties of the early neutrinos. Moreover, the observed signal may not solely be a gravitational wave background; rather, the Universe's early phase transition might also be contributing to it. Interestingly, the observed signal strength could potentially shed more light on the energy threshold for this transition. Interestingly, the observed signal can also be used to place certain constraints on the early phase transition energy threshold. Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest for the research community due to its unique capabilities and diverse range of applications. A significant feature of commercial plenoptic cameras, the lenslet array captures spatial and angular light information in a single exposure without the need for additional captures. However, the resulting high data transfer rates and intricate signal representations present significant processing challenges, particularly when employing modern deep learning techniques. To effectively utilize deep learning for light field technology, novel data representations and architectures that account for the distinct properties of light field signals are required. We introduce a novel light field representation called the 4D-PLF and develop an associated neural signal reconstruction model. The PLF representation separates spatial and angular factors to enhance feature extraction, and by leveraging these factors, we introduce a novel 4D-PLF generative adversarial network architecture. The novel PLF-GAN model supports end-to-end neural light field signal reconstruction from any 4D-PLF signal representation. Experimental evaluations using both real and synthetic datasets confirm the performance superiority of the PLF-GAN model over state-of-the-art light field signals and neural image reconstruction approaches.

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two fundamental models, 
interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings presenting themselves in each scenario. Non-interactive
models utilize pre-computed embedding spaces, separating document and query spaces,
while interactive models dynamically generate question and document embeddings 
synchronously during retrieval. This study innovates, introducing an interactive
model where the document embedding space is dynamically adjusted after each document
retrieval, in addition to question embeddings. This is achieved through a translation
head that concurrently produces a translation vector for a given document, in 
addition to proving theoretical bounds for retrieval accuracy, speed and memory usage. 
This is backed by experimental evidence, illustrating a balance between precise 
retrieval and processing efficiency, with the model performing competently on 
existing IR benchmarks.

The urgent need for comprehensive health and demographic reports has driven an increased focus on geographic studies, incorporating detailed, spatial data and demographic maps, examined previously by Alvo and Nellis (2013). Typically, studies rely on randomly sampled designs, which might not accurately represent the required information. To overcome this limitation, the use of informed sampling methods, such as stratification, has been employed, and recent techniques combine multiple methods to create hybrid designs. This paper introduces a novel algorithm, named ADDraw, that identifies the most suitable weighting procedure for studies with any random design, and is compatible with a wide range of models. The ADDraw algorithm examines a set of study conditions, identifies inconsistent estimates, and implements a weighted averaging method to produce a unified result. The study presents a comparison of different approaches, and claims that, for the first time, the ADDraw algorithm allows weighted averaging to produce reliable estimates under specific assumptions. The study's findings suggest that, in cases where these assumptions are met, weighted averaging demonstrates superior performance. Furthermore, the ADDraw algorithm's performance in non-robust scenarios has been assessed. The study provides a practical examination of how to apply the ADDraw algorithm, and demonstrates its practical application using real-world data from the Boston Area Community Health Survey. The survey covers a diverse range of topics such as obesity, smoking, physical activity, and medical insurance status. The use of informed sampling designs and the ADDraw algorithm have been shown to produce reliable estimates, and identify areas

The objective of this study is to propose a semi-classical model representing betting situations where the gambler's winnings are encoded in a quantum memory's intrinsic properties, rather than the conventional payout. We associate the initial investment with a single quantum system's ergotropy - a measure equivalent to the quantum analogue of free energy, as described by Allahverdyan, Balian, and Nieuwenhuizen - and compare it to both the classical betting scenario and the quantum breeder animal model.

Building on the recently created two-dimensional semiconductor MoSi$_2$N$_4$, our comprehensive study of monolayer compounds MA$_2$Z$_4$ involves in-depth analysis of their band structure and excitons using ab initio GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation calculations. In contrast to the predictions of density functional theory, the results of our GW calculations indicate much larger band gaps and quasiparticle energies that are distinct in absolute value but share the same band alignment configurations.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

The magnetic field and non-ideal factors are known to be pivotal in the process of stellar formation and initial planet formation, particularly in the development of molecular hydrogen gas. Consequently, suggestions have emerged that cosmic rays and weak radio emission from young stars may potentially trigger a significant change within the outer regions of a forming star system. Initially, this modification was found to have a substantial impact on the overall composition of the disk, prompting an examination into the broader consequences. Subsequent analyses revealed that inner regions of the disk, characterized by the protracted presence of small grains, might also be susceptible to the effects of non-ideal factors. The interaction of the magnetic field and vertical movements of the gas within the disk was discovered to have a notable impact on the sedimentation process of the smallest particles. In contrast, the mass flux was found to have a greater influence on the longitudinal dust transport, leading to a complex interplay between the magnetic field and vertical dynamics. Ultimately, simulations indicated that non-ideal factors can either facilitate or impede the vertical dust transport, depending on various factors involved. The possible scenarios include a reduction of vertical dust transport, triggered by the interaction of the magnetic field and vertical currents, or, on the other hand, an enhancement of vertical dust transport, caused by the mass flux and magnetic field. The predictions made suggest a substantial and complex impact of non-ideal factors on dust processes in the disk's structure.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is crucial.

This paper employs a refined hierarchical latent variable model to capture patterns in multi-period time series data, which exhibit dynamics governed by various time-sensitive factors. Traditional stacked RNN and DBN models lack the capability to incorporate tendencies spanning multiple periods and, therefore, often demonstrate diminished performance on datasets characterized by long-term dependencies. In contrast, the proposed LVH model, which leverages hidden states of multiple periods to generate observations, effectively captures multi-period relationships, yielding superior performance on datasets with long-term relationships. Furthermore, the model's architecture and learning process are designed to facilitate real-time inference and learning, which can be trained using conjugate gradient optimization with a limited number of iterations, even with large, high-dimensional datasets. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that the performance of the LVH model is comparable to that of the conventional Bayesian Gaussian Process model, which is known for its high computational demands.

In a setting that combines continuous logic, we establish a connection between Stone duality and Pontryagin duality by treating Pontryagin duality as a particular instance of Stone duality. This is achieved in the context of a topological abelian group $A$, and its associated group $\mathcal F$ of continuous homomorphisms from $A$ to the circle group $\mathbb T$, where $(A,+)$ along with $\mathcal F$ form a continuous logic structure $M. Consequently, the local type space $S_\mathcal F(V)$ directly corresponds to the Pontryagin dual of the group $\mathcal F$ if $V$ represents a compact abelian group, and further, this framework subsumes the Bohr compactification of any topological group within it.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results conducted on the Adult and Bank datasets demonstrate the "empirical" fairness of models trained with the new framework, in addition to the "theoretical" fairness of models trained with differential privacy.

A long-time favorite theory, the "Sneezing Supersymmetry" model involving R-parity leakage has been revisited. In this revised framework, a newly introduced right-handed neutrino acts as the dark matter reservoir. This model utilizes the 'intrinsically' R-parity leaking mechanism driven by the right-handed neutrino's seesaw interaction, which couples to the dark matter. On top of that, two slepton flavors experience R-parity leakage through a Type III two-Higgs doublet operator. In this model, we'll focus on two low oxidation level scenarios: 'Dark Matter near a Logarithmic Peak', which can accommodate both low and high dark matter masses, and 'Pure Adiabatic Tunneling', which requires a lighter dark matter mass. Both cases can evade current dataset constraints and offer a potential explanation for $(g-2)_\mu$. Furthermore, we'll highlight the underlying theoretical justification for this model to naturally generate a dark matter mass through the R-parity leaking mechanism by using 'Geometric SUSY' terminology.

We investigate a smart reflecting surface-aided wireless-powered communication network where a multi-antenna energy transmitter broadcasts an exclusive energy signal to a powered transmitter that initially absorbs the energy, then sends an information signal to the destination despite potential external interference. To optimize this setup, we've formulated an analytical problem focusing on maximizing throughput through the simultaneous optimization of energy absorption duration and reflecting surface phase shift matrices, despite this: the problem is complex and computationally challenging due to a significant number of variables, each with multiple associated constraints, and an intermediate optimization variable with an inherently non-convex nature. To address this, we've first established that the optimal energy absorption duration occurs early in the energy absorption period, then isolated this factor to yield an optimized solution. Next, we've dissected the phase shift optimization problem into two sub-branches, each with an associated matrix: one focusing on maximizing the determinant of the combined receive signal matrix and the other focusing on maximizing a corresponding lower bound. To optimize this second problem, we've leveraged an iteratively-tightened conic programming approach, starting with a conventional conic optimization algorithm, then applying a subsequent rounding process to yield an optimized solution. Finally, via numerical simulation results, we've demonstrated that our proposed solution, despite offering guarantees only for lower bounds of performance metrics, can still yield superior throughput performance compared to conventional solutions.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of prolate and oblate configurations independently in the parent and daughter nuclei. Prolate components dominated both parent and daughter nuclei for the experimental beta strength, while an upper limit was set for the oblate component in the parent state. To analyze the data, a new method for examining X-ray gated total absorption spectra was developed due to the analysis's complexity.

We explore the intersection of dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified theoretical framework, which includes three right-handed neutrinos, a fermionic dark matter particle, and two additional scalar fields beyond the Standard Model. The interaction between these scalar fields influences both the dark matter relic density and the connection between right-handed neutrinos and dark matter. Our analysis centers around a resonant leptogenesis mechanism that produces baryon asymmetry through TeV-level right-handed neutrino masses. A viable parameter space is established to satisfy relic density constraints, which is particularly flexible when the scalar fields' mixing is substantial. Our findings demonstrate that dark matter in this model can not only mitigate baryon asymmetry but also amplify it through the process of dark matter annihilation into pairs of right-handed neutrinos, even when dark matter is less massive than its right-handed counterpart. This amplified effect is contingent upon the dark matter and right-handed neutrino masses, $m_{\chi}$ and $m_N$ respectively, allowing for increased baryon asymmetry when $m_N$ equals 800 GeV.

We have designed a novel control method using learning algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information about the dynamics, such as basic physical laws and the system's general properties. The algorithm essentially finds the best possible solution to an optimization problem by gradually improving its objective function with the help of additional goals drawn from reinforcement learning. This control method has widespread potential applications in fields like medicine and space exploration. To test the algorithm's effectiveness, we used it to control highly complex 3D models of two medical devices and a spacecraft, successfully navigating the inherent uncertainties and imperfections in the simulations.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is visibly present as a Lie algebraic structure that arises from a specific type of supersymmetry and also a modified form of classical wave equation. A recently developed formula for the partition function of states in Toda conformal field theories, including priors to existing theories, reveals a heightened level of symmetry. A closer examination of this partition function reveals it is a type of free field correlation function that includes a modified version of the Wess-Zumino theory. This model's wave equation, a higher spin version of the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation, is found to be a fundamental part of the symmetry. The symmetry can also be seen in a specific type of operator correlation functions that include priors to existing theories. A deeper analysis using the "FFR" method reveals a clear link between the Toda deformed Knizhnik-Zumino equation, the higher spin Virasoro operators, and a modified form of the Toda deformed wave equation. This relationship provides a clear explanation for the Toda symmetry.

Despite significant advancements in producing realistic images with GANs, a primary concern persists, particularly for high-resolution inputs and intricate datasets, due to training instability caused by a mismatch between the real and randomly generated distributions, leading to a common issue of vanishing gradients during GAN training. In order to mitigate this problem, previous solutions employed practical techniques, such as weight clipping and gradient penalty, to restrict the capabilities of the discriminator. In this research, a more systematic approach is presented as an alternative to tackle this problem by focusing on relationships between paired samples rather than classifying them as real or fake. Specifically, a relation network architecture for the discriminator is explored along with a specially designed triplet loss that yields superior generalization and stability. Extensive evaluations conducted on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method, consisting of a relation discriminator and novel loss function, results in notable enhancements in a variety of tasks, encompassing unconditional and conditional image generation, and image translation.

A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been proposed. 
This method builds upon the concept of twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) in order to cater to the needs of point-to-point connections. 
Unlike other implementations, the phase locking device is not required, and to achieve this, we present a generation method for unconditional privacy-computed bound states.
The practical implementation of this idea involves deploying quantum superdense-coding resources in conjunction with quantum switching resources.
Using experimental data from a 485km-long experimental test bed, we've been able to demonstrate that TF-QKD without phase locking is possible, and we've also calculated a long-term key generation rate of 19.08kbps.
This breakthrough enables quantum communication over long-distance fiber, while also paving the way for the development of practical quantum superdense-coding and quantum switching applications.

In this study, we investigate the Toeplitz algebras of particular classes of Toeplitz operators on the p-Fock space and the p-Bergman space with 1 < p < ∞.  Let BUC(ℂⁿ) and BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) represent collections of uniformly bounded and continuous functions on ℂⁿ and ℬ_ᵐ (ℂⁿ's unit ball) respectively.  On the p-Fock space, it is proven that the Toeplitz algebra, having translation-invariant, closed BUC(ℂⁿ) subalgebra symbols, can be linearly generated by Toeplitz operators with those symbols.  On the p-Bergman space, the Toeplitz algebras having BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) subalgebra symbols are studied, and particularly, the generation of Toeplitz operators with BUC(ℬ_ᵐ) symbols is established.  The algebras in question are then equipped with involution operations, resulting in being commutative.

Despite significant advancements in object detection, current methods have limitations in detecting diverse object categories due to the labor-intensive process of creating training data with bounding-box annotations. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods have been developed to address this limitation by using reference categories for detecting novel objects. However, their effectiveness is constrained by the need for sufficient training data for background objects and multiple object categories. This paper presents a new approach called FeatPose that enables pose-based object detection to tackle the challenge of novel object detection. By leveraging pose-based associations between objects, FeatPose can detect objects in diverse categories without requiring unique models for each category, taking minimal supervision for a single category. Furthermore, FeatPose can be integrated with existing object detectors to enhance their capability for novel object detection. Experimental results confirm the superiority of FeatPose over state-of-the-art methods in novel object detection, with results on HPose53, PVANET, and MultiPoseGuide that show improvements of 24%, 47%, and 63% in terms of mean average precision.

A young B star in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud produces a significant HII region and a photodissociation cavity, forming in an egg-like shape. This cavity is primarily restricted on the west and southwest by a dense molecular cloud ridge and is expanding into a lower density area on the north and east. Analyzing a variety of recent and archival data from SOFIA, GMRT, APEX, and other telescopes provides detailed information on photoionization, photo-dissociation, and thermal gas. Uniformly distributed HII region straddles the Rho Opiuchi star field, with no noticeable ionization on the west side due to the cavity's border. Unipolar dust emission pattern suggests a helical magnetic field structure. East of the star, carbon emission from ionized carbon and carbon condensates correlates with hydrogen emission, indicating that the HII region straddles the Rho Opiuchi star field, with no noticeable ionization on the west side due to the cavity's border.
