The remarkable achievements of Transformer models in natural language tasks have piqued the interest of computer vision experts to explore their potential applications in visual tasks. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, Transformers rely on minimal inductive biases in their design, making them ideally suited for set-function applications. Moreover, their straightforward architecture allows for seamless processing of diverse modalities such as images, videos, and text. Due to their strengths, Transformer models have shown promising results in various computer vision tasks, leading to a growing interest in this area. This review aims to provide an in-depth overview of the current state of Transformer models in computer vision, focusing on the underlying principles and applications that contribute to their success. A comprehensive comparison of the advantages and limitations of prominent approaches will be presented, in addition to outlining promising research directions and substantial challenges that need to be addressed in this emerging field.

Mortality modeling through spatial prediction is crucial for understanding deaths caused by factors such as diseases, environmental conditions, and economic status. This modeling is further complicated by the influence of temporal variations, cyclic patterns, and unexpected events that impact mortality rates over time. In this research, a novel Bayesian spatio-temporal model has been developed using a locally constant surface framework, incorporated with a temporal process driven by seasonable and sudden changes. This approach makes it possible to incorporate autoregressive trends, dynamic structure, and district-level anomalies into the model, while also enabling the incorporation of prior knowledge and expertise. This methodology is further enhanced by the implementation of two computationally efficient procedures: the marginal-sampling around the interwoven Monte Carlo EM algorithm and the shrinkage-based method for estimating the hyperparameters. This model has been rigorously evaluated on two distinct datasets, including data from the African Region of the World Health Organization, suggesting that it effectively captures the complex spatio-temporal variations in the datasets.

Reducing the cost of neural architecture search (NAS) by sharing operators between child models is an efficient approach, but currently, it doesn't provide a guarantee for reducing the total search space size, and it doesn't guarantee a linear relationship between the number of shared operators and the reduced search space size. In an attempt to solve this, a new architecture sharing strategy is proposed to facilitate a linear decrease in the search space size and the expected training cost. By proving that the search space size decreases linearly with the number of shared operators, and the expected training cost at each step decreases linearly with the ratio of shared operators to total operators, the work offers a more efficient way to conduct NAS. According to the proposed strategy, a parent model is divided into two child models with shared operators, and their topologies are evaluated. By analyzing the relationship between the interference on a shared operator and the number of different operators, the search strategy dynamically adjusts the number of shared operators. As a result, the search strategy can efficiently reduce the search space size while keeping the expected training cost low. In experiments conducted on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, the proposed strategy is shown to achieve better search efficiency, and the searched models yield stronger performance when compared to other NAS approaches, and the default architecture.

Time series data in various scientific disciplines are analyzed and measured. One common technique for evaluating the characteristics of these data sets involves computing multiple statistical measures or features, which can then be represented as a feature vector for analysis. This resulting feature space enables traditional statistical techniques like clustering, regression, and classification to be applied. Multiple open-source libraries are available to extract these features, including ones written for languages like Python and R, but they come with challenges such as a lack of single unified access point, need to switch languages, and limited supporting methodologies for analysis. This paper addresses these issues with an R-based tool called theft. This tool creates a unified framework for computing features across multiple popular feature extraction libraries and also offers feature selection analysis. As an example of its capabilities, it demonstrates how to use these features to train and evaluate a supervised clustering algorithm. This tool, along with its documentation and source code, can be accessed at https://github.com/sdass/theft.
We identify concrete, infinitely precise criteria under which a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space has a semistable fundamental group at its boundary.

Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively utilized method that helps gauge machine translation efficiency, negotiate translation contracts, and evaluates human translator proficiency.  Despite its importance, little research exists using deep learning in TQA, which remains a traditional, subjectively-based process.  In our study, we investigate the application of a deep learning model using BERT to evaluate the quality of translations provided by human translators.  Our findings indicate that, similar to other multimodal deep learning-based systems, the TQA system exhibits high reliability and consistency among expert reviewers.  However, there is room for improvement in consistency among non-expert reviewers.  Moreover, we discovered that, unlike typical multimodal deep learning systems, the shared, semantic understanding among human translators does not significantly impact the TQA system's performance.  Ultimately, this research highlights the potential benefits of using deep learning in human-assisted TQA, as well as significant avenues for future exploration related to machine-based TQA.

In our investigation of random systems that scatter across broad areas, such as those found in certain types of nanomaterials and living tissues, we have developed an innovative approach for quantifying the deposition of light or other propagating waves. Our framework generalizes this deposition matrix to encompass various physical phenomena, including electromagnetic, acoustic, and quantum particle transfer. We have derived a set of wave-like equations that satisfy conservative boundary conditions, and our analysis shows that the deposition matrix arises naturally from the scattering process. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the deposition matrix is linked to probability distributions of wave energy in the system. We have further developed methods for estimating the deposition matrix from experimental data, including a real-time, continuous probability current formula, which has the advantage of being linear even in complex scattering environments. Our findings offer a new pathway for experimentally measuring scattering probabilities in complex media that may also apply to the study of quantum particle transfer.

We've found that using pruning methods on artificial neural networks significantly
reduces their size while maintaining their performance, and can even reveal smaller
sub-networks with higher accuracy than their full counterparts. Our study focuses
on understanding the inherent biases of these "lucky network subsets." We looked at
the effects of iteratively pruning a basic neural network on a specific type of task,
finding that the remaining connections create localized patterns. Our analysis
suggests that data influences the structure of the pruned networks. The characteristics
of the pruned networks are surprisingly similar to those of manually-designed neural
networks, opening the possibility of automating the process to discover more
efficient network configurations for a variety of tasks and data sets.

In lotteries with exceptionally large jackpots, as seen in Powerball and Mega Millions, multiple winners often share the prize. To understand the value of a lottery ticket in this scenario, we calculate its expected return under two assumptions regarding ticket value. When there is a high likelihood of multiple winners and the prize pool is small, our model indicates that the expected return on a $1 lottery ticket approaches $0.95. However, if there is only a slim chance of shared winnings, the expected return on a $1 ticket is roughly $0.60. The variation in expected return on a $1 ticket can be explained by a ratio that compares the odds of a single winner to the number of tickets sold. Our approach leverages techniques from measure theory, using an integral representation to determine the expected return on a lottery ticket. Additionally, we derive a criterion to determine when the normal approximation is suitable for estimating the expected return on a lottery ticket.

The large-charge expansion technique opens up a new possibility for calculating critical properties of high-charge operators $\phi^Q$, where the charge $Q$ is fixed. For operators of a given charge, the mathematical structure of their critical properties can be determined in the weak coupling regime by performing a series of calculations at fixed $Q$. When calculating at the six-loop level, new and complex diagrams that involve five or more legs need to be taken into account - these were previously unencountered in theoretical scalar-field calculations. Our research involves finding the critical properties of an operator with charge $Q=5$ at the six-loop level, complemented by existing information for operators of smaller charges. Furthermore, our results allow for a more precise estimation of critical properties of the model than would have been achieved through a conventional expansion in the critical $q$ parameter.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we observe that two mechanisms, cone tilt
and deformation potential, yield analogous effects on valley Hall responses.
However, this equivalence does not apply when the coupling involves position-dependent
velocity of electrons. The presence of a significant valley Hall effect near a
neutral charge condition in the isotropic scenario mirrors that seen with changes
in bond lengths, while in the anisotropic scenario, geometric transport of valleys
is diminished similar to what is seen with deformation potentials.
Additionally, introducing strain variations leads to total inhibition of valley Hall
transport even when accounting for the dynamic behavior of these strains. The use
of a gate voltage allows for control over the valley Hall effect, paving the way
for exploration of new properties and functions in valley acoustoelectronics.

The VisDA 2022 Challenge seeks unsupervised domain adaptation for industrial waste sorting in semantic segmentation tasks, where we proposed the SIA_Adapt model. Combining several domain adaptation methods, SIA_Adapt's key strength lies in extracting transferable representations from extensive pre-training datasets, allowing for adapted features and pseudo-labeled targets to be generated through self-training. Subsequently, SIA_Adapt refines the adapted features by using the pseudo-labeled targets through a decoupled structure consisting of a feature extractor, classifier, and inference-reversed classifier. Moreover, SIA_Adapt simulates semantic confusion through dropout and noise during self-training, ultimately producing pseudo-labels that account for the adapted domain's semantic shifts. Furthermore, SIA_Adapt uses the mean teacher method in conjunction with self-training, enabling the adapted domain's knowledge to be incorporated and refined. At VisDA 2022, SIA_Adapt's multi-stage approach earned it a 2nd place ranking (78.2 mIOU), and we highlight its effectiveness using PytorchVisDA-Citiessc dataset, https://github.com/VisDA-Challenge/VisDAChallenge, and provide additional SIA_Adapt models on https://github.com/Alaei-Hosseini/SIA_Adapt.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. This article investigates how the presence of label correlations impacting data geometry influences t-SNE analysis. It develops a systematic framework to estimate these correlations by utilizing t-SNE and demonstrates a relevant case study involving a dataset with structural labelling, showcasing how the incorporation of these labels modifies the assumed proximity model, thereby altering the effectiveness of the t-SNE technique.

We investigate the characteristics of the two-dimensional Fermi polaron model, where a single impurity is attracted to a sea of Fermi particles under strong attractive conditions. Our findings are determined through an accurate variational method that incorporates the exact ground state of a similarly defined one-dimensional model. Initially, the polaron exhibits a transition from an extremely weak to an intermediate interaction regime before evolving into a bipolaronic state under extremely strong attraction. This intermediate regime shows significant agreement with variational estimates of a effective medium approach. Additionally, the variation in the polaron's effective mass, with and without electron-electron interactions, across various attraction strengths is thoroughly examined.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum simulation, a complex, variable interconnectivity relationship exists between qubit gates and target operators. We investigate an optimization method to simulate a fermionic system's dynamics by accurately applying the fermionic swap operation between qubits. Through an analysis of this operation's properties, we have determined the most effective connectivity arrangement for qubits to efficiently simulate a chain of fermions and have specifically analyzed the impact on simulation precision for different numbers of qubits paired with varying levels of paired ancilla qubits for coherence. We discovered the highest simulation precision is achieved with a topology of qubits connected as a ferromagnetic chain and have specifically looked at the pairing of qubits with two ancilla qubits for coherence. This topology is also naturally suited to quantum simulation of spinful fermions due to the spin-swapping operation's ability to efficiently mimic the fermi-hubbard model's interaction terms, though this requires an additional ancilla qubit for coherence.

Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their potential to develop algebraic formulas describing various graph characteristics and encoding multiple graph invariants through their evaluation processes. Certain graphs, including complete and bipartite structures, can be identified through matching polynomial properties and relationships with established polynomial sets. The chromatic polynomial evaluated at -1 reveals the count of a specific graph orientation type. This study focuses on a general theorem involving families of graphs, which can be characterized through polynomials with established linear recurrence relations. This finding provides numerous applications in characterizing similar graph types, and offers an alternative to using complex polynomial sets in favour of a simpler linear relationship approach. The work highlights the distinct capabilities of graph polynomials in describing various graph characteristics.

We derive an expression for the pullback of the Hitchin connection, extending from the moduli space of genus two curves to a 10-fold cover of a Teichmueller curve, which was first studied by Veech. Subsequently, we develop an expression in terms of iterated integrals that describes the monodromy representation of this connection. Consequently, as a secondary result, we determine the quantum representations of a vast array of pseudo-Anosov elements in the genus two mapping class group.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining individualized support with autonomy to achieve enhanced Scrum home working effectiveness. Moreover, we establish that support and autonomy can effectively enhance working from home outcomes even without providing structural support. These findings offer valuable insights to managers who lead or collaborate with remote or hybrid Scrum teams.

The concept of dichotomous matrices serves as an expanded interpretation of Hermitian matrices, with newly formulated guidelines identifying which arrowhead matrices fit this classification. Furthermore, specific conditions were derived to ensure unitary irreducibility of these matrices, and their maximum orthonormal vector count in relation to boundary numerical range was examined. Additionally, connections between these matrices and others were compared, including Popov nonnegative matrices and Yafarov matrices.

In a study using the ALICE detector at the LHC, scientists investigated the elliptical movement of electrons created when beauty particles decay at a specific point near the centre of a collision between lead nuclei at a high energy of 5.02 TeV. These electrons were observed within a narrow region and the researchers found that their movement followed a specific pattern. Using a unique characteristic of beauty particles that decays at a longer interval than many other sources, scientists were able to isolate this specific type of decay and measured its movement. They found that this specific type of decay exhibited elliptical movement. Their findings were then compared with a theoretical model that suggests that beauty particles interacted with the medium in a complex in a complex scenario but the researchers couldn't get a clear conclusion due to limited data. However, its different from previous findings on lighter quarks.

In pursuit of breakthroughs in the medical field, we analyze chromatic configurations in three-dimensional space, employing topological concepts. Leveraging techniques borrowed from image processing, we develop mathematically sound indicators to capture both fine-scale and broad-scale interplay among color categories. Our proposed methods enable fast computation and are densely-data-driven, distinguishing them from traditional Euclidean embedding techniques that necessitate positive edge weights. To evaluate the robustness of our approaches, we test them across a range of synthetic and real-world datasets.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to observed binary power control superiority in typical, non-asymptotic, sparse systems.

Auditing business processes often requires categorization of data, which can be efficiently done using supervised machine learning techniques. However, the black-box nature of some machine learning models hinders their trustworthiness. This paper focuses on developing a gray-box categorization method, offering transparency and explainability. The method combines the strengths of different machine learning models, including logit enhancement, decision trees, and support vector machines, and utilizes a multi-objective optimization approach to determine the most suitable method. The proposed method excels over traditional non-explainable machine learning methods in categorization tasks. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach through the analysis of real-world data from two Austrian auditing companies, and shows that the performanc e and explainability of the method can be controlled through specific parameters. The method's availability has been realized through the development of a software tool, which is presented at AUML 2022.

The Strauss process is a point process, and its density is unnormalized relative to a Poisson point process, incorporating a weighting factor lambda, between zero and one, which is applied to each pair of points closer than a certain distance, denoted as 'r'. Traditional techniques for simulating this process involve an accept-reject approach but a new method utilizes a perfect simulation technique, thereby ensuring fixed simulation times. However, the current perfect simulation algorithm has significant computation complexities such as exponential random variables and high-dimensional integration. A more efficient approximation of the Strauss process has been developed with a simpler representation, offering a trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency.

In the context of string theory and quantum gravity, the Generalized Uncertainty Principle revealed the presence of an inherent minimum length, confirmed through the deformation of Heisenberg's algebra. Utilizing this concept, the paper explores quantum mechanics with a state-dependent metric. It defines particle wave functions recursively and redefines Schrödinger's equation for a free particle across different metric regimes, leading to the identification of an inherent minimum length. Additionally, the paper computes the GUP parameter's magnitude for any arbitrary momentum and finds that it significantly increases with momentum, approaching a critical value, thus confirming Heisenberg's algebra's validity for high-energy particles. It also demonstrates that particle positions cannot be measured below a certain scale, effectively establishing a fundamental minimum length. Furthermore, the paper examines the effects of metric deformations on bound states in the hydrogen-like potential and reveals that although length scales may vary across different systems, the GUP parameter's magnitude remains distinct for each potential type. It successfully reconstructs the quasi-confining potential consistent with the GUP, making this system a viable candidate for exploring quantum mechanics and the minimal length with bound states.

Multitasking scheduling in service industries has gained significant interest due to workers frequently transitioning between tasks. Building on Hall, Leung and Li's 2016 model for shared processing multitasking, this research extends the model to a more complex setting with parallel machines. Unlike the original model, where a set fraction of processing capacity is allocated to routine jobs, this extension allows for varying fractions of routine jobs' processing capacity to be assigned on each machine. The primary objectives remain the minimization of makespan and total completion time. Unfortunately, it's demonstrated that solving these problems optimally using polynomial time unless P=NP if machine ratios are fully adjustable. Conversely, if machine ratios are fixed, these problems can be solved in a timely manner. Furthermore, this research invests in developing heuristic methods for these more complex scenarios.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the challenge of effectively navigating through deformable terrain environments. This challenge is further compounded by the tensor-valued permittivity and conductivity fields present on the terrain's surface. Developing suitable regularization methods is essential for efficiently simulating the fluid-structure interaction between the deformable terrain and the walking robot. This study introduces an adaptive numerical approach for regulating terrain surface dynamics and integrates it into a trajectory optimization framework for a five-link hexapod walking on a deformable surface. Notably, simulations demonstrate a substantial decrease in integration errors, specifically by a factor of 10, when using the presented method. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates a high level of adaptability, even when the terrain's motion frequency is significantly higher than the robot's step frequency.

In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Things (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are vital for maintaining optimal security and reliability. Given the trend towards implementing security measures via codified policy decisions and exchangeable code (security-as-a-code), these updates should become standard practice. However, deploying firmware updates across vast numbers of IoT devices poses a significant challenge, particularly in large-scale distributed settings. This study examines how to efficiently and reliably distribute firmware updates to a large number of IoT devices over non-terrestrial networks. To measure the success of these updates, we establish a set of Quality-of-Service Key Performance Indicators, and leverage self-regulating feedback mechanisms, specifically Multi-Ararm Indexing Algorithms, to ensure optimal network usage and minimal energy consumption in both satellite and terrestrial networks. By integrating these mechanisms, we ensure that, in cases of network failure, backup networks can support the update process, and maximize the overall number of devices updated. Furthermore, we explore several strategies for prioritizing device updates, with a focus on first responding to critical devices, and utilizing fuzzy logic for prioritization. This study evaluates the success of these mechanisms through real-world scenarios and case studies, and verifies that a fully functional IoT network can be restored following a large-scale attack or network failure.

We employ a recursive Green function approach to obtain the Fock space propagator and associated self-energy for one-dimensional interacting fermions in a disordered system. Our results show that the local self-energy's imaginary component, which governs the decay rate of initially localized states, can serve as a probabilistic phase transition order parameter, facilitating the characterization of critical behavior and multifractal properties in many-body localized states across various disorder regimes. Moreover, we establish that the fractal dimension associated with the local self-energy experiences a discontinuous change at the phase transition, where it jumps from less than one in the localized phase to one in the thermal phase. Furthermore, the local self-energy's asymptotic scaling behavior in the vicinity of the critical disorder strength displays two distinct modes: an exponential growth in the localized phase, and a power-law variation in the thermal phase, with a critical exponent related to the system's fractal dimension. Our results also reveal that the phase space volume explored by an initially localized state grows logarithmically with time in the localized phase, whereas it grows linearly in the thermal phase, with a critical factor related to the system's fractal dimension.

To make the most out of human insight in solving interactive graph problems,  our kBM-IGS framework leverages both board games insights and machine learning.  The kBM-IGS (k Best Moves Selection) problem involves identifying the most effective initial k moves within a board game's board, which a player can utilize to maximize their winning potential.  Our framework allows a combination of human and machine intelligence,  where a board evaluation function, inspired by chess techniques,  estimates the value of the board following each possible move.  Additionally,  through analysis of the MinMax algorithm search process,  our model can pinpoint the most crucial board positions influencing the value of the board.  Our method was tested successfully on PegSolitaire,  a traditional board game.  The outcomes show that our technique allows both effective initial move selection and accurate board evaluation.  The PegSolitaire environment was even used to train a neural network for general board games applicability,  which could serve as a starting point for applying such an approach to more complex games like ConnectFour,  Reversi,  etc.

The exploration of quantum machine learning has demonstrated the potential for
groundbreaking insights in both areas of research. Experimental findings indicate
that quantum computers could significantly outperform traditional machines in
certain machine learning tasks, although they may also be susceptible to
adversarial threats. These threats involvequote;noise; or unanticipated inputs that
degrade the quantum model's accuracy. Although some quantum-based methods to
mitigate these dangers have been proposed, they are narrowly focused on specific
scenarios. This study presents a generative quantum model called q-Gaussian
Mixture Model, representing a general class of Gaussian mixture models, which
leverages the benefits of kernel methods. It applies a variant of the Quantum K-Means
algorithm, leveraging the capabilities of near-term quantum computers to develop
probabilistic models without relying on classical data preprocessing. Through
simulations using real data, it successfully discovers Gaussian mixture models
without relying on quantum classification. This study also provides estimates for the
probability of adversarial examples affecting the model that can be compared to
classical counterparts through numerical simulations. These findings support the
idea that quantum machine learning can provide unique solutions to machine learning
challenges.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues in nearly spherical domains of three dimensions.  Building on our earlier research, which demonstrated the eigenvalues to be analytic functions of domain perturbation parameters, we calculate the first term in the asymptotic expansion in relation to Wigner 3-jsymbols.  Through analysis of the asymptotic expansion, we establish the isoperimetric theorem that if 'l' is a square number, the 'l'-th eigenvalue attains its minimum at the sphere.  This research includes a comprehensive analysis of the spectral gap between consecutive eigenvalues, which remains positive until a specific threshold of domain perturbation is reached.  We show this threshold corresponds to a specific case of a minimal surface embedded within a sphere when considered up to three-dimensional isometries.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data.

Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models are broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic models. Empirical models, although computationally simple, are often inaccurate due to oversimplifications in their statistical basis. In contrast, deterministic models, like those based on ray tracing and measurement-based approaches, provide precise wave interaction data but incur computational complexity. This limits their practical application. We combine the strengths of both types to develop a novel hybrid propagation model. The core of this model involves a ray tracing-based estimation process that addresses angular dependence and scattering effects, followed by a statistical adjustment to account for unmodeled channel aspects. Initially validated with IoT layer channel measurements, this approach holds significant potential for enhancing various wireless channels simulations.

A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL, and then obtain a validation algorithm based on that semantics. By using a formal Isabelle/HOL proof, it is shown that the validation algorithm faithfully represents the developed semantics. We also demonstrate through practical experiments that the verification of our algorithm is useful.

Power system expansion planning models, used to integrate renewable resources, rely on complex optimization problems involving various economic and technical factors. These factors carry significant uncertainties, yet their impact on model accuracy is poorly understood. This study introduces a new approach to assess the sensitivity of power system models to specific parameters by measuring the increased costs resulting from inefficiently locating generator capacities. Through case studies involving wind dispatch and transmission investment, the model's sensitivity to varied parameters is evaluated. Results show that social welfare, transportation costs, and transmission capacity are highly sensitive to specific parameters, whereas capital expenditures and CO2 emissions have lower sensitivity. This research highlights the need to assess model performance across a range of parameters to inform investment decisions.

This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a particular reflection scenario for the Vlasov equation.

When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely written requests for change, described using everyday language and involving relevant technical terms. The task requires identifying key terms related to the request's technical context, allowing developers to locate relevant sections in the source code and apply the desired changes. Unfortunately, developers often struggle to craft effective search terms for their tasks. This paper presents a new approach, STRICT, which uses machine learning and information retrieval to automatically determine suitable search terms based on a change request's description. The proposed method leverages two techniques: TextRank and POSRank, both relying on a novel stopword elimination technique that utilizes a technical dictionary to preserve crucial terminology during the search. Experimental results on two industry datasets demonstrate that STRICT surpasses current best practices, yielding higher recall rates, specifically 58.2% versus 52.6% for Tetris and 42.3% versus 39.6% for Git. The study's findings indicate that STRICT outperforms existing tools, suggesting that further research is needed to refocus software exploration from source code to project documentation.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic vibrations. This sensitivity allows the gels' mechanical properties to be fine-tuned through external sound waves, which significantly impacts their ability to support weight under stress. When ultrasonic vibrations reach certain frequencies, the rheo-acoustic gels transition into a state of reduced stiffness, whereas increasing the sound wave intensity yields varying outcomes in terms of stress. To better understand the chemical makeup of these materials, researchers created model systems from polymers and surfactants that can be tailored to have specific component ratios. Scattering experiments have revealed the effects of ultrasonic waves on the structural makeup of these model systems, which suggests that ultrasonic vibrations cause particles to move more freely and lose their temporary structures. This phenomenon is linked to the dynamic interactions between the particles as they approach one another, which is influenced by the particles' reduced effective size and viscosity. Ultrasonic waves may also create unique patterns of temporary structures that emerge at specific intensity levels, which is characterized by the particles' altered hydrodynamics. To clarify the relationship between the chemical makeup of these materials and their response to ultronic vibrations, researchers analyzed a system of polymer and surfactants with varying component ratios and observed the effects of ultronic vibrations on their mechanical properties. Which is to say that the chemicals in the gels affect how they interact with stress and pressure when ultronic vibrations occur.

This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements, which is then generalized to encompass all positive odd integers. By applying the principle of mathematical induction, this extended set is used to prove the conjecture. A second verification of the conjecture via mathematical induction is also presented in section 9. Consequently, the conjecture is validated through a duplicate approach, and both generalizations of the conjecture are confirmed. Notably, the first generalization provides the formula c(n) = (2^(2p-1)+2^p) mod m, where n is represented as 2p mod m for any integer m greater than 1, while the second generalization is defined by the formula n = (m/3)+r, where r is a remainder when m is divided by 3. A table has been included to illustrate the results of the conjecture for certain values of m and n. A second form of the conjecture, the natural language version, has been presented in section 9. It is suggested that the results of the conjecture should be tested using higher-powered computers, such as those used in the ATLAS computational software, which is also mentioned in the conclusion along with a few unrevealed findings.

To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a particular field, precise categorization of document subjects is crucial. Currently, classification primarily relies on human expertise to create and apply classification systems, but we believe that computers should play a more significant role in this process. Our research focuses on enhancing the accuracy of scientific classification using computational methods, particularly for STEM disciplines. We argue that in these areas, precise categorization is crucial but often hindered by the subject's rich mathematical underpinnings, which are inadequately represented in current classification systems. To address this, we suggest creating mathematical entities to represent different subjects, measuring their presence in documents, and developing a new classification approach based on these findings. Our experimental results reveal that classification based on mathematical entities leads to more accurate outcomes and better subject representation than existing models.

To guarantee matching among all agents, the Deferred Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that stable matchings are achieved even with shorter, albeit incomplete, preference lists, thus sparking curiosity as to why and how agents should optimize limited preferences for the best possible matches. Researchers have made significant headways in understanding this concept, and our work further explores this idea, focusing on developing an approach - Deferring - where agents can effectively obtain optimal matchings from their limited preferences. We found that, contrary to existing theories, our proposed method can indeed yield suboptimal results under certain circumstances, and we cannot guarantee its convergence in all cases. Consequently, we have established stricter criteria necessary to guarantee a successful match using the Deferred technique.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they are
highly unreliable in assessing human quality and limit the potential for
improvement through data augmentation. Consequently, a new metric called SummScore
has been developed to evaluate the overall quality of a summary. This innovative
approach, built with a pre-trained language model, measures summary quality across
four key dimensions - grammatical correctness, natural language use, coherence,
and relevance. By effectively capturing human quality and yielding lower
inter-annotator variability, SummScore has proven its value in machine-generated
summaries.

A new method for extracting a sparse signal from cross-related data is presented. This type of signal can be the source of images in hybrid imaging techniques, which combine optical and radio wave information. To make this problem more manageable, we only need to calculate the cross-correlation matrix's diagonal, rather than the entire matrix. To take advantage of this property, we developed a practical solution with a built-in ability to perform zeroth-order optimization, and we also developed a more efficient version that uses a specialized approach, providing a feasible solution with useful results. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we used a model of a 2D signal affected by noise and other disturbance factors, and we were able to extract the signal's details, verifying our recovery results with accurate measurements. This method can be applied to various types of signal, and we included the relevant mathematical proofs in the appendix for further reference.

The conventional approach to 3D object detection, where camera and LiDAR data are combined, is no longer tenable in realistic scenarios due to its vulnerability to LiDAR malfunctions. This has restricted the use of these models in practical autonomous driving applications. Our novel fusion method, called BEVFusion, stands out by not requiring any input from the LiDAR data, thereby addressing this limitation. Our results demonstrate that our method not only surpasses current standards in regular scenarios, but it also outperforms them significantly in environments that mimic real-world LiDAR malfunctions. Specifically, our method shows a substantial gain of 15.7% to 28.9% in terms of mAP when compared to existing solutions. To date, our method remains the first of its kind to tackle real-world LiDAR malfunctions effectively. The code supporting this work is available at https://github.com/ADLab-AutoDrive/BEVFusion.

We are reassessing Turbulence's Third Law to better understand thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluids. Previous studies determined the characteristic length scale, $\ell_{+}\propto \eta_+$, is proportional to the Kolmogorov length scale, $\eta_+$. However, our new investigation indicates that $\ell_{+}$ should be linked to the Kolmogorov length scale, $\ell_{K}$, applied to the high-energy range of the spectrum. When this principle is applied, it leads to the following expression for the spectrum $E(k)$ that is valid across a broad range of scales and energies: $E(k) \propto k^{-2}$ in the high-energy range and $E(k) \propto k^{-5/3}$ in the low-energy range. Moreover, it is predicted that $E(k)$ will be determined by non-linear processes in the high-energy range and by linear processes in the low-energy range. These predictions were based on simple models for energy transfer and thermal fluctuations, however, it is confirmed that they are also compatible with direct numerical simulations. It is also found that the simulation results suggest a link between the $E(k)$ spectrum and the structure that is characteristic of the inertial range in the Kolmogorov-Obukhov spectrum. Previous studies on laser propagation through a heated fluid employed simplified thermal conductivity and convective heat transfer assumptions, leading to inaccurate predictions. This study presents an in-depth numerical analysis that accurately simulates the thermal behavior of the fluid and its impact on laser interactions. The study examines the diffracted beam in the far field produced by a laser entering the fluid, as well as the interferometric pattern formed perpendicular to the laser propagation axis. The results are validated against experimental findings, providing comprehensive insight into laser energy transfer and propagation through the fluid. The study observes and elucidates the spatial self-phase modulation and laser propagation control that can be achieved through controlled diffraction effects, ranging from small-phase diffraction to aberration-controlled diffraction and diffraction oscillations.

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relating to software design for knowledge accumulation. This is achieved through a process known as design mining. Recent breakthroughs in this field utilized supervised learning, but are limited due to a lack of a standard dataset and inconsistent sample sizes. This paper introduces DeepDS, a novel dataset containing 13,726 design-related comments from multiple software projects. Furthermore, we propose a standard evaluation protocol for design mining data analysis. Additionally, we present a novel model, LIM-DSD, based on a type of computer network that outperforms previously used models in terms of accuracy, recall and f1-measure.

This paper presents a novel evaluation engine for big stream and data processing pipelines called H-STREAM. It integrates stream processing micro-services with relational database management systems to develop cloud-based event processing platforms. H-STREAM boasts five main features: 1) decentralized stream processing using independent micro-services, 2) micro-service reconfiguration and relocation, 3) directed acyclic graph-based event processing pipelines, 4) reliable event processing, and 5) stream-to-query integration. H-STREAM supports stream-to-stream and stream-to-query integration methods. It utilizes micro-service reconfiguration and relocation to handle stream processing activations and deactivations, and directs actived stream processing micro-services. H-STREAM also handles micro-service activations and deactivations for event processing activations and deactivations on its event processing graph. It utilizes micro-service activation and deactivation to handle event processing activations and deactivations on event processing graphs. During failure events, H-STREAM's stream processing micro-services activate redundant micro-services to ensure event processing reliability. Furthermore, H-STREAM's integration with relational database management systems provides stream-to-stream and stream-to-query integration methods. An experimental evaluation was conducted using actual big data and processing pipelines, showing the benefits of H-STREAM's cloud-based event processing platform. It surpasses other platforms in several aspects, including latency, reconfiguration frequency, and event processing reliability. The hunt for Top and Bottom companions is a key area of study for both the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as their single production offers considerable detection possibilities. Though past research mainly focused on the resonant production mode of these hypothetical particles, new findings have uncovered a diverse and complex phenomenology associated with the non-resonant diagrams at narrow widths. In this study, we thoroughly examine the influence of the non-resonant diagrams on the single production topologies of Top and Bottom companions and their impact on estimating total production rates. We also present an simplified framework to evaluate the non-resonant contribution and illustrate its application with representative example scenarios.

A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating SPARQL query generation, but these models have a major limitation: they can only handle queries based on knowledge that was learned during training. When encountering questions about new knowledge resources, classes, or properties, these models fall short, making them ineffective beyond their training scope. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel framework called Questo that builds on zero-shot translation to address this challenge. By translating questions related to unknown knowledge into queries about known knowledge, Questo enables zero-shot query generation. The experimental results showcase that our approach succeeds in generating correct and relevant SPARQL queries even with unknown subjects.

This work introduces a novel method for systematically categorizing and assessing the quality of diverse publishing outlets in Computer Science. Leveraging a substantial subset of the extensive DBLP dataset covering over five decades, our technique evaluates millions of contributors and thousands of publishing venues based solely on available paper publication information. By treating authorship patterns at individual publishing venues as stochastic processes, our qualitative metric captures the quality of each venue. Experimental results reveal that this measure aligns with expert subjective evaluations and current objective quality indices. Moreover, our technique enables the detection of potentially reputable yet underrepresented publishing venues, thereby facilitating diversity promotion. Furthermore, our method facilitates the estimation of author and institution reputation based on venue scores, providing new insights and complexities in evaluating scholarly production. Our comprehensive method is fully accessible through a web-based application, allowing users to explore and query the calculated venue scores. The corresponding web platform can be accessed at https://scholarship.cs.ntu.edu.sg/.

Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant analysis difficulties regarding the safety of control systems. Fortunately, recent research has introduced methods for analyzing and verifying the complex control systems. This tutorial synthesizes and introduces techniques for verifying the robustness of neural networks that originated in related fields. These techniques are further applied to establish guarantees for systems that combine neural networks and control feedback loops. Ultimately, these tools are employed to analyze the stability of neural network-based controllers and ensure the safety of the resulting control systems.

This work builds upon three significant lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering: the pioneering work of Jardine and Sibson, the development of Markov chain-based methods, and the application of graph theory frameworks. Our research aims to integrate these disparate threads into a comprehensive clustering theory grounded in graph theory, with a particular emphasis on its theoretical underpinnings.

Visual data recovery from partially observed tensors is the focus of tensor completion. This process aims to recover the missing tensor elements based on its observed components and underlying structure, described through its low-rank factorization. This aim is articulated as an ill-posed inverse problem, addressed by regularizing it with strict constraints on the tensor's structured factors, rather than the tensor itself. This shift highlights that the recovery process involves trading data fidelity for restored tensor accuracy. We examine two classes of constrained regularization methods. First, we investigate and evaluate intrinsic spectral techniques using Krylov subspace approximations. We demonstrate that the inherent spectral methods utilizing Krylow approximations are equivalent to applying gradual, iterative low-rank constraints. Moreover, we show that the iteration count directly correlates with the degree of low-rank constraints applied to the restored tensor. Second, we introduce an innovative scheme to impose low-rank constraints in tensor completion using rank-reduced linear measurements. We demonstrate that direct regularization of factors is equivalent to regularization of measurements. To evaluate the performance of these methods, we performed a comprehensive numerical study, analyzing their behavior during convergence. Additionally, we applied them to various real-world datasets, highlighting their recovery capabilities for video, audio, and biological data applications.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the conjugacy classes of classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$ and $W(D_{n})$ take the form of type D. This finding has implications for the Nichols algebras associated with irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules over the classical Weyl groups $\mathbb W_{n}$, revealing that these algebras have infinite dimensions, with the exception of three distinct cases: the $(2, 3),(1^{2}, 3)$ case in $\mathbb S_{5}$, and the $(1^{n-2}, 2)$ case in $\mathbb S_{n}$ for $n >5$.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of the downscale cascade. Focusing on scenarios with strong and weak external forces, they analyzed the resulting turbulence and found support for an inertial wave turbulence model. A related theoretical model was also developed, based on conventional weak turbulence methods, and compared to the simulation data, providing further evidence for the downscale cascade. A key distinction was drawn between true wave turbulence and geostrophic turbulence which, despite its name, was shown not to exhibit downscale energy cascades.

We investigate a basic model called Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN) for analyzing weighted graphs, and a variation of this model called Linear Programming for Graph Normalization (LPGN) that produces an exact linear programming solution within a timely framework. By selecting an optimal combination of maximal independent sets, IGN and LPGN achieve two-degree graph normalization with no parameters that need adjustment. Moreover, IGN and LPGN facilitate the analysis of weighted graphs through the primal-dual junction tree algorithm. In the context of Homogeneous Minima Surfaces (HMS), we utilize IGN and LPGN to evaluate a dynamic graph average, specifically a weighted mesh triangle count, and further refine a mesh regularization method. By integrating IGN and LPGN into an extension of the parameterization method, we achieve a novel parameterization technique called LP-TPS. Our research showcases the efficiency of IGN and LPGN through a combination of computational and experimental results presented in this paper.

This research studies the impact of a magnetic field on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, aiming to understand the effect of modulation on the thermodynamic properties. The findings reveal that electric modulation has a notable influence on Landau levels, resulting in an asymmetrical Landau level spacing, unlike in a conventional 2DEG. Furthermore, we find that while some thermodynamic properties exhibit similar behavior to a 2DEG, there is a significant difference in the behavior of the specific heat and magnetic susceptibility.

Recent findings have identified low-frequency radio emission from systems consisting of small cool stars called M dwarfs, which shares similar patterns to magnetospheric phenomena observed in our Solar System. The radio emission could be driven by a star-planet interaction or an unstable balance in a rotating stellar wheel of gas and dust, known as a protoplanetary disk. The early detection of such radio emission could provide valuable insight into the formation of such systems. Additionally, the radio emission could be produced by charged particles interacting with the star's magnetic field, producing a detectable signal around 10-50 MHz. A new study aims to explore the possibility of detecting radio emission and changes in the early activity of stars using a device called the TIANO instrument, which is designed to test and demonstrate various scientific techniques. The instrument is planned for use in a star-observing mission called SPECFold and will specifically look for radio emission and changes in activity using a different technique than current space missions, such as the VLA Sky Survey. The study involved simulating various noise sources and tested the ability of the SPECFold instrument to detect radio emission and changes in activity. The test indicated that the SPECFOLD instrument should be capable of detecting radio emission and activity changes with its current design, although actual detection rates may vary based on specific astronomical targets and observational conditions. The SPECFold instrument's sensitivity to radio emission and activity changes should allow it to provide valuable new insights into the formation of exotic planetary systems and early

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges for realistic virtual
human avatars, we developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new framework that
extends DNR. In experiments and user evaluations, ANR consistently outperformed not
only DNR but also other avatar creation methods, including those based on physics
and observations, demonstrating its superiority in creating visually engaging and
realistic virtual humans. Further research could enhance the realism of ANR by
incorporating additional factors, such as eye movement and lighting interactions.

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate aspects of primates' and humans' neural performance. However, these ANNs primarily rely on basic visual characteristics when performing object recognition tasks, unlike humans. Additionally, ANNs are hindered by unusual or misleading input, whereas humans' learning and reasoning capabilities enable them to withstand diverse and uncertain visual input. We propose a novel set of object recognition challenges, aimed at evaluating the effectiveness of human learning and visual representation, as well as the ability of ANNs to facilitate human-level visual understanding. The custom-made database, featuring 300 unique objects, accompanies the test battery to assess visual representation and learning capabilities. Our study demonstrates that humans demonstrate robust object recognition across the challenging conditions, whereas ANNs struggle, despite reaching high accuracy in the initial simple tasks. The test battery and dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/bl-b/Visual-Object-Recognition-Challenge.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory, along with its relationship to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant, which uses quantum algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{su}_2)$, is examined in this exploration. Certain tangle diagrams associated with three strands that include a spin-$1/2$ closed loop demonstrate a connection to the AW algebra's generators. Both the Chern-Simons theory and the Reshetikhin-Turaev construction show that the link invariants generated by these tangles adhere to the algebra's generator relationships. This reveals that the Chern-Simons theory's expectation values for Wilson loops satisfy AW algebra relations and the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariants fail to differentiate between equivalent linear combinations of links.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which effectively tackles the thermodynamic properties of frustrated two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnets composed of loosely connected three-spin clusters. Specifically, we investigated the thermodynamic behavior of a strongly breathing distorted kagome lattice model and the previously proposed triangle-square lattice model relevant to La4Cu3MoO12, leveraging a trimer-cluster based computational basis to minimize the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem at low temperatures. Our analysis extends beyond the thermodynamic properties to examine the mean field theory prediction of a phase transition associated with chiral order. We observed a two-peak structure in the specific heat for the breathing distorted kagome lattice model in both the quantum spin liquid and lattice-nematic regimes.

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, users can instruct these models to classify sentiment with untrained examples by prompting them with reviews paired with labels such as "Does the user like this movie?" The disparity between the input and target languages can be mitigated through "meta-tuning". This technique entails training a pre-trained language model on a parallel corpus, effectively aligning its perception of words across the two languages. By doing this, we discovered a 16% improvement in zero-shot sentiment classification accuracy for English film reviews and a 7% improvement in accuracy for Spanish film reviews. Additionally, meta-tuning facilitated the translation of movie titles from English to Spanish without altering the original text, yielding satisfactory results according to an intrinsic and intrinsic evaluation.

In depth research into the likelihood and characteristics of a robust first-order electroweak phase transition has been carried out as a prerequisite to studying electroweak baryogenesis within the context of the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM, considering recent data from the Higgs sector, dark matter searches, and analyses from the Large Hadron Collider involving both strong and weak interactions. A detailed examination involved implementing the $T$-$T_{CP}$ plane in the $T$-$S_{\phi}$ plane, with results indicating that while the NMSSM can potentially accommodate a robust first-order phase transition, this possibility is constrained by constraints arising from the Higgs sector, dark matter searches, and collider searches, thus implying that no parameter sets can satisfy both theoretical and experimental requirements. Furthermore, theoretical investigations into the sources of baryogenesis during the phase transition revealed that while the NMSSM can accommodate baryogenesis through weak annihilation, this process may have difficulties occurring due to the presence of light stop tunnelling, thus reducing the likelihood for successful baryogenesis through this process.

We introduce novel approaches for visually identifying reliable redshifts through emission lines in the millimeter and submillimeter spectrum. Our methodology involves evaluating the effectiveness of diverse millimeter and submillimeter observational methods in measuring spectroscopic redshifts and optimizes future observations to maximize the proportion of robust redshifts. To facilitate this process, a publicly accessible code is shared at (https://github.com/tjlcb/redshift-search-graphs). We discuss scenarios in which robust redshifts can be confidently identified through single-line or multiple-line detections, as well as instances where redshift ambiguity persists despite multiple line detections. Our analysis leverages the redshift distribution of millimeter and submillimeter samples to assess the efficiency of various observational practices, including those utilizing interferometers and dedicated instruments designed for redshift searches. Finally, we outline an optimized observation strategy for the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to achieve robust redshifts in the z = 2 - 4 region, with specific importance placed on 2 mm wavelength measurements.

This research uses large-scale matrix-product state simulations to determine the capture of the antiferromagnetic spin-1/2 $J_1$-$J_2$ model's most stable phase. A detailed study is conducted on how the $120^{o}$-ordered phase's captured area responds to $J_2$ under the presence of $J_1$-hole perturbations. As $J_2$ increases beyond $J_1$, the $120^{o}$ phase declines and the model enters an nematic meta-stable region. When evaluating how $J_1$-hole perturbations impact this system, the findings suggest that correlation materialize in localized triplets even with moderate levels of hole doping. Moreover, the presence of non-magnetic singlet states formed due to doping cause the quantitative decline of the $120^{o}$ phase's captured area. In contrast, the complex interplay of magnetic and non-magnetic correlations gives rise to an emergent nematic phase which initially emerges in low-doped $J_1$-$J_2$ models as a stable phase. A detailed investigation reveals the subtle interplay between magnetic triplet and non-magnetic correlations occurs at a very low doping level. As a result, the emergence of the nematic phase appears to be heavily dependent on whether it undergoes a smooth process of doping or experiences it through quantum annealing.

The study explores lattice cutoff effects on the phase transition in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory across four dimensions and their implications on $Z_3$ symmetry, where a complex triplet Higgs boson has no initial mass and interaction. By regulating lattice size through variations in $N_\tau$, the investigation reveals that the phase transition depends significantly on this regulation, notably at $N_\tau=1$ and 2, and demonstrates qualitative differences with $N_\tau=4$ when employing the same lattice spacing. Moreover, to minimize lattice effects, a rescaling approach is implemented to compare simulations at distinct $N_\tau$ values, and findings suggest that the $Z_3$ symmetry may be intact during the phase transition, thus allowing for a study sensitive to the lattice cutoff. Finally, based on rescaled observations, the phase transition in the model appears to be a second-order confinement-deconfinement transition, independent of the lattice cutoff.

Cr$_2$Al is investigated as a potential ferromagnetic material for spin thermal rectification devices, which rely on a ferromagnetic-based redshift phenomenon to convert spin waves into heat above the N\'{e}el temperature. Through various measurements, a N\'{e}el temperature of 100 K is confirmed for Cr$_2$Al, as it approaches the working temperature of these rectification devices. By examining the electronic structure of Cr$_2$Al, it is determined that it exhibits a half-metallic nature, which is in line with the parameters of an exchange coupling constant (D$=1.0\cdot10^{18}$ J/m$^3$) and a magnetocrystalline barrier strength (R$=3.0\cdot10^{20}$ J/m$^3$). This suggests that the material is highly suitable for spin-based rectification devices. Furthermore, micromagnetic simulations of spin wave propagation indicate that the N\'{e}el parameter variation in this material is sufficiently pronounced to demonstrate a redshift phenomenon. As a result, the design of a spin thermal rectification experiment, which uses a ferromagnetic Cr$_2$Al material, is proposed. It is estimated that with a specific parameter choice, a Cr$_2$Al-based device could efficiently convert 60% of spin heat. A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. By integrating relaxation-time approximation, the $
u$-model's collision frequency becomes velocity-dependent, thereby incorporating essential collision characteristics from Boltzmann's equation, while also reflecting the influence of the target velocity distribution function, akin to the Shakhov model. Following numerical simulations of strong non-equilibrium shock waves, a combination of theoretical and empirical methods is employed to develop a suitable velocity-dependent collision frequency for varying intermolecular potentials. As a result, the $
u$-model exhibits notable improvements in accuracy, along with a thorough examination of its underlying mechanism. Furthermore, the $
u$-model performs well in canonical rarefied micro-flows, particularly in thermal transpiration cases, where conventional kinetic models struggle with velocity-dependent relaxation.

Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge in NLP. The latest state-of-the-art semantic parsers employ sequence-to-sequence models, built upon vast language datasets pre-trained on a massive scale of text. Building on these advancements, researchers have explored redefining semantic parsing, resulting in naturally-phrased output sequences within limited language constructs. This breakthrough yields remarkable outcomes, particularly in few-shot learning scenarios, a critical area in practical application and the main focus of our study. To take this line of inquiry forward, we introduce a novel approach that combines the benefits of (i) pre-trained text representations, (ii) sequence-to-sequence decoding, and (iii) language-based constraints to enhance our output's grammatical accuracy and adherence to the input query semantics. The heart of our method lies in synthesizing two refined vectors: (i) one bolstering semantic representation and (i) the other leveraging language structure, which serves as a common anchor for our output sequence generator. We showcase our the efficacy of our technique, particularly in the area of few-shot learning, by achieving superior results on a leading semantic parsing benchmark. We make our code and model architecture openly accessible for future research development.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve leveraging a powerful electron-proton collider to expand our knowledge of heavy ingredients called quarks and gluons that make up matter, and to explore novel regions of energy. To achieve this, we must understand the creation of heavy particles such as charm and bottom that serve as indicators or "flags" to track their movement through a jet. To measure these heavy particles and jets, we will utilize a state-of-the-art detector designed to catch energy releases from the interaction, and to accurately reconstruct the movement of these energy releases. The development of a sophisticated instrument called a calorimeter that uses advanced materials to detect energy releases is crucial in this measurement. Future research at the Electron-Ion Collider will serve as a key testing ground for the development of cutting-edge instruments and advanced techniques that will improve our understanding of the behavior of energy releases in energy collisions.

A new discovery in X-ray variability patterns in four galaxies, including Mrk 104, M51, M60, and M87, has been made with the help of the NICER telescope and Soft X-ray Spectrometer. These patterns, named Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs), have frequencies ranging from 100 to 1000 times per minute. They differ from previously discovered Quasi-Periodic Oscillations (QPOs) in that their peaks decay over time. In the case of an accretion disk near a black hole or neutron star, QPEs tend to appear as short-lived, signature patterns. Analysis of the QPEs in Mrk 104, using various spectral models, has revealed a pattern of variability that points to the accretion disk near a few million kilogram black hole, with a specific pattern of pattern variability that matches the boundaries of an inner disk. It is suggested that the peaks represent the transfer of energy from an accretion disk wind to the inner disk, with the boundaries limiting the observable pattern of variability.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long sparked debate over their influence on the atmospheres of stars. Our research provides new evidence from spectropolarimetric analysis on how the strength of a magnetic field in HD58260, a magnetic star, decreases as you move higher in its atmosphere. The results suggest that the outer atmosphere has a magnetic field roughly one-third as strong as its inner layers. The increased flow of high-energy particles in magnetic fields near these stars could explain their surrounding magnetospheres and the high-energy events they exhibit. Our findings also identify a set of useful spectral lines that can be used to measure the surface magnetic fields of similar early-type stars.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

We derived an SFR of 0.077±0.009 M⊙yr−1 from the ALMA H30α measurements, but found that this value differs from the SFR derived from far-infrared and submillimeter observations by a factor of three to four.
