Our previous research significantly sped up the time it takes to solve semidefinite programming problems (SDPs) by introducing a new class of matrices with L/U-CoLT (Low/Upper diagonal with Elements on Transition) properties. The current computational processes for SDPs can take a long time, especially for larger matrices, leading to significant slowdowns. By building specialized data structures for matrices with this L/U-CoLT property and implementing efficient operations on them (in addition to standard L-CoLT and U-CoLT), we are now able to perform complex calculations quickly. For example, we can perform multiplication, division, and science operations in linear time, regardless of the size of the matrices. The resulting time savings for SDP solutions is substantial - we see up to 30 times improvement over the fastest previous methods. Furthermore, these matrices with L/U-CoLT properties have connections to other areas of study, including graph theory and optimization. As a result, we were able to quickly implement a new method of solving SDPs in half the time of previous methods, using a technical understanding of the 'dual SDP' relationship. Another connection inspired a novel procedure for solving the steepest descent direction of a non-convex optimization problem with graph-related constraints, yielding substantial speedups for large-scale problems.

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planets inside its debris disk, presents an extraordinary chance to study these impacts. Studying 93 X-ray emissions from AU Mic using the XMM-Newton telescope, researchers discovered variations in emissions, inferred magnetic activity cycles, and detected 15 ultraviolet emissions with the NuSTAR ultrasensitive X-ray optical system, revealing a correlation between X-ray and UV light emissions. Analyzing these findings, researchers used young star models to simulate how AU Mic's magnetic activity and planetary disk formation relate, offering valuable insights into planetary evolution.

We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an effect where the medium is warped by the motion of charged particles in a way that the Debye length remains a critical determinant for the energy lost through radiation. As a result, we find that the total energy lost through radiation, under these new circumstances, depends on the rate at which the particles interact with the medium, not just on their speed. We use two distinct models, one for overdamped and one for underdamped processes, to describe the vibration of the medium and derive a unified formula for the energy lost through radiation in both scenarios. We test the validity of our new description by applying it to a hypothetical scenario where the energy lost through radiation is measured, under conditions of thermal equilibrium and dynamic stability. We also explore the practical uses and limitations of our new theory, discussing its relevance to real-world situations such as the suppression of jets in quark-gluon plasma and the interaction of particles with surrounding matter.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem where one class
exceeds the others in population size, a standard classifier tends to generate
predictions that are biased towards the majority class. This issue highlights the
need for an alternative to traditional accuracy metrics, which have failed to
reflect the true performance of a system in an unevenly distributed classification
setting. In response to this limitation, a proposed new metric is introduced,
referred to as the calibrated confidence gap (CCG). This metric aims to
compensate for an unevenly distributed classification by focusing on the overlap
between the predicted class probabilities and true labels. Experimental tests using
 simulated and actual data have demonstrated the effectiveness of the CCG metric in
capturing the unique characteristics of unevenly distributed classification results.
Furthermore, a proposed remediation technique, which involves oversampling the minor
classes of data, aims to mitigate the predicted bias towards the majority class.
Experimental results indicating the successful utilization of this method have been
observed.

We employ photometry data from multiple sources to identify ultra-bright Quasi-Stellar Objects (QSOs) located at distant regions of space. By utilizing SkyMapper's DR3, along with 2MASS, Gaia, and other existing datasets, we combine them with new photometry obtained from an ongoing SkyMapper survey to build a comprehensive photometric catalog. This extensive catalog permits the creation of the most extensive photometric color-magnitude diagrams in our study for QSOs across seven distinct redshift ranges from approximately 3 to nearly 7. We derive the QSO luminosity function for a specific type of intrinsically luminous QSOs, describing their brightness with a power-law distribution, and we observe a change in this distribution's slope as changing from approximately 3 to nearly 7 in redshift value. We further determine that our QSO catalog matches other surveys in terms of their number and flux consistency when comparing our findings on local QSO density across our redshift ranges with those from the Gaia DR2, and we report an additional 152 new QSOs discovered in this process in our multi-band photometric catalog which is accessible at: https://cosmo.skymap.eu/journal-articles/2022/2/

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible subgap energy states. Our findings offer valuable insights for future research focused on detecting parity-dependent interactions between these quantum dots and superconducting islands, potentially revealing the existence of elusive Majorana modes.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. To expand upon existing work, we investigate the behavior of strong shocks in various models and systems, including fluid flow and electromagnetic phenomena. Furthermore, we devise a framework to validate the existence of infinitely stable strong shocks and provide a theoretical framework for analyzing the dynamics of these shockwaves. It is found that these strong shocks behave similarly to infinitely stable shocks in a particular model, as concave smoothing of the solution does not change the average location of the shock front. Consequently, the dynamics of these strong shocks can be described using a dynamic equilibrium equation, which describes the movement of the shock front over time. Moreover, we investigate the dynamics of these strong shocks when the shock waves interact with each other, as in the case of the initial formation of the shock wave in certain models, and provide a theoretical framework for analyzing the dynamics of these interacting shockwaves. It is found that the dynamic equilibrium equation accurately describes the dynamics of these strong shocks and provides a theoretical framework for analyzing the dynamics of these interacting shockwaves.

We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen views by virtually navigating a given image -- through a new, promising approach. Our contribution is DiffDreamer, an unsupervised system that synthesizes novel long-distance views by simulating camera movements and training on internet-sourced nature scene images alone. Our results confirm that conditioned diffusion is more effective than previous generative methods in generating extended, unseen views, allowing for high-quality view generation at various distances. When compared to conditional GAN techniques that also employ camera movements, our approach approximates the generated views with similar accuracy, albeit at reduced computational cost. Finally, our research details challenging scenarios for generating novel long-distance views and highlights the significance of collecting a large, diverse training dataset covering a broad range of camera positions and perspectives.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the cooperative effects of random complex dynamics, fewer studies have explored the role of stochastic nonlinear systems. This study demonstrates stochastic nonlinear complex systems can produce robust, cooperative effects on a large scale, analogous to those in stochastic linear networks. Unlike their stochastic linear counterparts, however, stochastic nonlinear networks rely on a specific distribution of agent nonlinear functions to produce this cooperation. This research involves stochastic nonlinear discrete-time and continuous-time systems as well as a model of glassy tempers, illustrating diverse examples of cooperative behavior in stochastic nonlinear networks.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to investigate the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from a study conducted by Haefner, et al., published in 2015 in Nature Communications.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two human evaluators measured and compared the coronal image deformity angles acquired from both robotic and manual scans. The results showed that robotic scanning yielded highly reliable results both within and between evaluators, with minimal difference compared to the manual approach in terms of coronal deformity angles. Furthermore, robotic scanning exhibited excellent within-evaluator reliability. Robotic scanning also demonstrated equivalent efficacy to manual scanning in identifying mild scoliosis curvature. This study suggests that robotic scanning is a reliable alternative for evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as reduced statistical variability and robustness to training data irregularities. This approach is beneficial in speech synthesis as it enables the production of natural-sounding durations with mean values that can change over time and potentially converge to target values. We assess the effectiveness of our model using speech with varying lengths and find that it outperforms a established model based on hidden Markov models. Furthermore, experiments with a synthesis-by-multiplication method that combines the proposed duration model with an energy-based speech synthesis system demonstrate the potential to improve naturalness and naturalness-constrained speech quality without compromising on data rate efficiency.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. It was discovered that models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in how they allow subnetworks to learn and share features. In response, we introduce an innovative 'unmixing' procedure for MIMO networks to facilitate shared feature learning among subnetworks. Our preliminary results demonstrate the efficacy of this modification, yielding feature sharing and better performance in smaller network configurations.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents through image-based techniques. Specifically, this involves exploring datasets designed for image processing tasks including text extraction, line segmentation, and feature extraction which collectively aim to restore academically significant documents in their original format. A thorough examination is conducted into 11 datasets, evaluating aspects like data source identification, data licensing, website hyperlinking, data sampling (including the distribution of page numbers, words, lines, and binary pixels), data extraction, formatting, image processing, text analysis, and machine learning-based training, all with a focus on achieving accurate word, line, feature extraction, as well as the corresponding ground truth data for comparison purposes. Known datasets are identified and existing datasets are compared, and a new dataset is proposed to address gaps existent in current data sets. The proposed dataset is called the Document Image Bilingual Corpus (DocIBC) and is derived from documents written in two different languages. A significant advantage of this dataset is the presence of both languages in the document, enabling the performance evaluation of language identification models. Additionally, this dataset is unique as it boasts an impressive collection of images derived from 625 distinct document images, providing a substantial sample pool. Furthermore, this dataset is diverse, with varying levels of binary pixels, word extraction possibilities, and lines, rendering it an excellent candidate for testing the performance of classification models. Additionally, a novel, two-language document collection is developed that is inspired by the practical requirements

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory precision using supplementary sensors and a novel feedback control strategy in combination with a feed-forward approach based on flatness. For this purpose, a novel dynamic model is introduced that describes a mobile robotic joint as a mass on a sled with dynamic characteristics. A feed-forward controller is designed using the flatness theory to generate optimal trajectory previews. Subsequent to testing the proposed strategy on different types of industrial robots, it was found that the precision of the trajectory was improved by up to 90%, which made the robots suitable for high-accuracy machining applications.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. This perspective considers early life experiences and later lifestyle behaviors as interacting and influencing future health paths. Inspired by the examination of social life patterns, which involve analyzing changes in various aspects of a person's social life, a new research method is proposed that utilizes multiple time-related health data to identify distinct types of health trajectories. These types are then characterized by their ages of onset and completion, similar to how social types are defined by their transition patterns into and out of different life stages. This new method aims to identify unique clusters of individuals based on their individualized health development paths, utilizing a maximum variation approach to find representative types. Next, the distribution of age values for each type is estimated using a non-parametric method, allowing for the calculation of type probabilities. This new research method is then applied to two real-world datasets to examine the types of health development paths present.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at each atomic site, effectively dividing the integrand. Although the unaltered Becke scheme exhibits slow convergence when applied to free electronic states found in processes like photoionization, this modified version achieves efficient results comparable to those for bound states. To accomplish this, the modified scheme incorporates a unique transition mechanism where atomic weights are gradually deactivated at a distance of a few bond lengths from their respective atomic nuclei and replaced by a smoothly converging global weight, ensuring seamless integration of atomic site weights into a unified whole. This hybrid approach to numerical integration is applied to compute phase arrays for complex wave functions, essential for computing cross sections of complex molecular shapes. As such, it is ideal for use in computational methods that address the mathematical challenges posed by complex molecular scattering problems.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by the vertex cover number yielding fixed-parameter tractability. However, the complexity under different parameters remained unclear until our recent discovery, where the problem was found to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the feedback vertex set number. Additionally, we found that parameterization by the vertex cover number results in the problem not admitting a polynomial kernel unless a significant assumption holds. While the problem remains open under the vertex cover number, we found fixed-parameter tractability when parameterizing the problem by distance to cluster or co-cluster.

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a distinctive low atmospheric heating pattern. Research into this phenomenon is complicated by a lack of experimental data and inconsistent model outcomes, including discrepancies in the African Saharan region of various models. This study involved conducting extensive simulations using a high-resolution model to study the hydrological cycle of a stable climate with stable atmospheric conditions and a healthy water cycle, similar to modern-day Europe, as a benchmark, and a simulated 'hothouse' climate with enhanced atmospheric heating and increased water demand, and a weaker hydrocycle, similar to what has been observed in some models for a different 'hothouse' climate. The difference between the two was analyzed and various model outcomes were evaluated for how well they described the system. The results, and implications for future simulations and understanding these unstable climate states, are discussed.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we confined the twistor functions to zero-spin and added a source term, it matched the conventional Yang-Mills theory. Introducing a non-zero spin source enabled us to derive self-dual Yang-Mills theory. This method also uncovered an unexpected twistor action for Yang-Mills theory that only depends on its magnetic properties.

The current dominant approach relies heavily on a substantial number of cleanly labeled samples for effective training of medical image classification models. However, the reality is often marred by noisy labels introduced during the labeling process, which have far-reaching consequences for real-world medical image classification. This work presents a robust method to eliminate the influence of noisy labels on the training of medical image classification models. The method is built upon a commutative merging strategy for the training and validation process, where susceptible noisy labels in the training set are cautiously removed and replaced with new, improved labels. The method's efficacy was tested across eight robust optimization scenarios, each with varying levels of noise percentages, and against a range of state-of-the-art adversarially trained models. The results showed that at a 20% noise rate, our method outperformed all other methods, achieving a 4% improvement in validation accuracy. Notably, our method consistently performed on par with models trained using adversarial training methods, but at a significant cost reduction of nearly 25%.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and an explicit formula is given for the characteristic polynomial of the CRW's transition probability matrix, utilising a determinant expression related to the graph's generalized weighted zeta function.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome to use, we present an alternative based on lambda abstraction, making it possible to define any termination condition as a function in this manner. Furthermore, by utilizing function application normal order, any clock mechanism is unnecessary when defining recursive functions, allowing us to define a common agreement function on arbitrary sets. Moreover, we demonstrate how to define a non-terminating function using a clock with an dynamically set depth limit.

The accuracy of models predicting the Reynolds dependence of wall-bounded flow's skin-friction drag, such as the Kolmogorov-Zakharov model and the model developed by Kalchev, Kim, and Lumley, is assessed based on the existing data from direct and indirect numerical simulations. It is observed that the potential of these models to predict the zero-repeated-scale aspect of the wall-bounded flow's velocity structure functions, a crucial factor since the information about higher-repeated-scale aspects is limited, varies with different types of flow. For turbulent flows in channels and pipes, the models show promising results but may not be accurate for smooth-walled, laminar flows in certain cases. Furthermore, it is suggested that the simplest form of the Kalchev, Kim, and Lumley model could be modified by incorporating a factor dependent on the local Reynolds number rather than just the average Reynolds number. This modification appears to be true for turbulent flows in channels and is a hypothesis for further investigation.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field behavior. The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an energy lower bound, with corresponding self-dual equations whose solutions manifest as the limiting solitons that achieve this bound. The lower bound on energy, known as the Bogomol'nyi bound, exhibits proportionality to the topological charge of the Skyrme field, thereby being quantized. Conversely, the total energy is bounded from below by a function dependent on charge and gauge charge, with the former being quantized while the latter loses its quantization in the overall bound. Moreover, this work showcases spherically symmetric self-dual solitons within a reduced version of the baby Skyrme model that includes both gauge and Skyrme fields, with the solitons losing their quantized nature within this scenario.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has an orbital magnetic flux of $p/q$ with $0\le p \le q-1$, we studied its phase diagram under minimal crystalline symmetry. The results showed the existence of various phases: phases containing multiple Weyl nodes with surface Fermi arcs; a Chern insulating phase featuring gapless surface states despite bulk gapping; a unique phase combining gapped, topologically non-trivial bands with gapless Weyl nodes, connecting to a Chern insulating phase; and a new gapped phase exhibiting non-topological, counter-propagating surface states that could be isolated under the absence of crystal symmetry. We successfully found analytical solutions for phase boundaries applicable to all $p, q$ values. The results specifically predicted that properly choosing $p$ and $q$ values should enable realizations of both the gapped Chern insulating phase and the unique gapped, non-topological phase for $q=3$ without the need for $p=0$. Moreover, examining $q=3$ in the absence of $p=0$ should serve as a test for discovering new, non-topological states for various materials.

This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, called a FOMix structure, combining features of Fano interferometry and metaverse resonators. When coupled with all-optical Kerr media, the FOMix device enhances light absorption in the system and redirects it outward in a controlled manner, increasing the overall radiation rate of the emitters. Consequently, the FOMix design offers substantial advantages over traditional methods for enhancing spontaneous emission rates. Additionally, the paper examines the spectral characteristics of the FOMix device and finds its resonances are predominantly influenced by the monopole and dipole modes, while also observing the emergence of complex multipoles in a limited parameter range. Furthermore, the FOMix design has potential applications in developing highly efficient light-emitting and light-absorbing devices.

Mechanical screening is a widely used concept in studies of both crystalline and amorphous materials. In this study, we apply mechanical screening to simulations of mechanical loading in amorphous solids, utilizing simulations of both compressed and stretched materials. Through a detailed theoretical examination, we clarify the distinction between strong and weak screening, showing that strong screening corresponds to a localized, thermodynamic average, whereas weak screening relates to a shorter-range, topological average. Furthermore, we demonstrate that strong and weak screening converge under conditions of either extremely high or low strain levels. The implications of our findings are considered within the context of recent research findings.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between hydrogenated and native metals. Furthermore, the system's dynamics is studied through second-order density-matrix perturbation theory, revealing differences in vibrational frequencies, charge densities, and drift moments between manganese/doped manganese and manganese/ hydrogenated manganese interactions.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to a significantly older, 10 thousand year estimate. Our objective is to create a straightforward simulation of a supernova event replicating the shape, dimensions, and placement of Sgr A East, which was achieved using a simplified hydrodynamic model that simulated the development of a supernova remnant within the vicinity of the Galactic center. This area comprises a close-by large molecular cloud with which Sgr A East interacts, and the wind from the galactic center's dense star cluster. According to our most preferred remnant models, Sgr A East's age likely spans around 10 thousand years. Additionally, the best fit for observations, excluding those of the southern cloud, indicates a supernova event expanding at a rate of 3.7 km per year. However, when including the southern cloud in calculations, the supernova event's rate increases to 4.2 km per year. Our simulations also show that Sgr A East may have begun expanding before first breaking through the galactic disk at around 3.3 kiloparsecs. A noteworthy outcome from our simulations is that the southern cloud, whose density is much greater than surrounding areas, significantly slows down supernova expansion. At 4.5 thousand years, the model with southern cloud contact shows a central cavity formation similar to the observed void

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. The outcomes suggest that using oversampling methods enhances the accuracy of random under sampling, and that SMOTE and its variants excel over random oversampling, indicating their potential applicability in real-world contexts.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by its national prevalence but ultimately became less correlated as other issues took precedence. Additionally, we found that some local news topics at the start of the pandemic were determined by factors such as government COVID restrictions, the local economy, and news outlet politics, and later by the school reopenings, lottery winnings, and baseball playoffs as other issues surpassed COVID coverage. Moreover, we found that local news COVID coverage was more prevalent in areas with higher COVID death rates, larger populations, and greater audience engagement with government, but this trend reversed for areas with significant COVID vaccination rates. Lastly, we found that local news COVID coverage was more prominent in cities with lower poverty rates, less unemployment, and greater audience engagement with politics. These findings highlight how local news COVID coverage is influenced by various standalone factors.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated and due to its nature, naturally maintains system variability. Although SPH incurs truncation errors from kernel interpolation that can be misconstrued as conservation violations, these errors don't breach total mass, momentum, and energy conservation; implementation of an accurate integration method and sufficient particle density stochasticity are crucial in preserving these properties. Historically, improper implementation of integration techniques has tainted the SPH method, portraying an incorrect perception that SPH inherently breaches conservation. Recent technological advancements in computing has enabled high-performance computing at achievable costs, allowing for the execution of sophisticated algorithms on simulated systems to rectify conservation breaches through additional stochastic forces. This thesis delves into conservation breaches and probable stochastic algorithms. It contrasts their conservative and stochastic properties, illustrates possible approaches to determining optimal stochastic parameters and explores the fundamental principles underlying stochastic algorithms. Furthermore, it examines thermodynamic principles and their implementation in SPH, concluding with a detailed analysis of the fundamental art of implementing stochastic algorithms in SPH to simulate thermodynamic processes.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of cross-sectional ratios in electron proton collisions, drawing on JLab polarization experiments measuring the ratio of Sachs form factors in such interactions. Calculations considering a scenario with fully polarized, in-line initial and final protons have been carried out to analyze polarization transfer and compare results with an experiment measuring double-spin asymmetry in another process. Research found a significant $Q^2$ dependence influence on polarization transfer to the proton, which may be exploited in new experiments to measure the $G_E/G_M$ ratio.

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced models. The policy cloning approach, a fundamental component of various learning techniques, is our focus, as it leverages the expertise of a guiding model to shape a student model's behavior. In order to accomplish this, we implement our proposed method, augmented policy cloning, which introduces artificially generated states to a training environment, making the system sensitive to its surroundings, thus greatly reducing the need for direct interaction with the environment for the learning model to perfectly replicate its mentor's behavior. We achieve highly efficient behavior mimicry by requiring our student models to learn how to interact with the environment in a way that precisely replicates the guide's actions, utilizing synthesized data to master environmental interactions that were originally learned by the guide through self-experimentation. We achieve optimal results by automating an environment-generating system, fitted to a static model image of a environment, to create images representing guides' actions and their corresponding states during training, thereby greatly reducing the need for interaction with a environment by the learning model. We achieve optimal results by pinning the generated data to a fixed memory size, making the system learn a representation that is not affected by changes to the guiding policy, thus allowing the system to switch between different guides with ease and a static representation of these states as a whole.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been carried out utilizing the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The research explores final states in which the vector boson decays into electrons and neutrinos or into electrons and other electrons and neutrinos, and each Higgs boson decays into pairs of $b$-quarks. It aims to detect the $Vhh$ signals from non-resonant and resonant production modes as well as from the triple-gluon process in next-to-leading order perturbative QCD. Prior to imposing any selection on the observed events, the study places an upper limit on non-resonant $hh$ production at 3.8 or 4.3 times the standard model's predicted rate for $W$ or $Z$ bosons. Furthermore, the study sets a two-sigma confidence level upper bound on resonant $hh$ production at 10.4 or 23.5 times the standard model's predicted rate for $W$ or $Z$ bosons. Finally, the study sets a two-sigma confidence level upper bound on resonant $hh$ production at 17.2 or 40.4 times the standard model's predicted rate for $W$ or $

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation, offer exceptional sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in the form of a all-optical electronic circuit combining resonant gain and loss with a drive field through gain-loss detuning, effectively modulates a resonant RF field and detects smallest magnet fluctuations.
We have developed a self-oscillating atomic magnet system combining the 87Rb atom gas cell, micro-heater, micro-optical system, micro-electronics, and micro-chip resistive sensors to instantly respond to external magnetic fields.
This innovative magnet system, designed with a compact square shape, presents a unique amalgamation of analog and digital technologies, and exhibits superior magnet sensitivity and dynamic range.
In particular, our self-oscillating atomic magnet system is capable of accurately determining magnetic field ranges from 0 to 100 mT with a 0.6 pT resolution, and effectively identifies magnetic field ranges while rejecting electronic noise and optical system instability.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model incorporating additional complex parameters in the hidden sector, leading to a significant impact on R-pariton masses, thereby allowing for a neutralino's delayed decay. The framework, denoted by 'HDMSM,' necessitates the introduction of a gauge field in the hidden sector, ultimately giving rise to a cosmic string network. We investigate the signature of these cosmic strings in the CMB and the radiation background's polarization, yielding a limitation on the neutralino's relic density through a cosmic string's relic density, where the model's parameter dependence largely originates from the cosmic string's annihilation.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface area enclosing rectangle surrounding a given simple graph, and extending this approach for general bounded-face graphs. Furthermore, a 2-approximation algorithm was derived for finding an enclosing rectangle with minimal diagonal diameter in bounded-face graphs. Additionally, semi-definite programs were implemented to obtain solutions, and in cases where the programs converge slowly, an exact algorithm based on integer programming was applied to yield highly effective results.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Furthermore, our project's data, which comprises hate and non-hate posts from Hindi and Bengali Twitter users, is made available online for public use.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the background expectations for neutrinos studied on large-scale detectors, and open the door to new research areas such as neutrino directionality and dark matter detection. A method for directional neutrino detection has been developed using a novel approach based on analyzing the nuclear recoil vector's projection onto the local vertical direction. This method requires designing an energy-dependent directional vector efficiency, however it does not rely on the specific geometry of the detector and can operate at high energies where the angular distribution of recoils is narrowed due to gravity's dominance. Applying this method to current and future neutrino experiments could allow them to set strict limits on major neutrino flavors' cross-sections under the standard model. Furthermore, this method has the potential to significantly enhance the ability of detector models like Borexino to detect dark matter, and can also serve as an alternative for Fermi-LAT and XENON1T data analysis.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. Based on a literature review and expert consultation, we identified crucial factors impacting driving behavior and designed an uncertainty-reflective questionnaire format to capture experts' diverse views. Fuzzy set modeling enabled us to incorporate these uncertainties into our analysis. The proposed method allowed us to incorporate contextual feedback from four key stakeholders: road safety experts, transportation engineers, data analysts, and business professionals. Our findings indicate that incorporating expert input modified their assessments of a driver's performance, as they were able to provide more accurate and consistent ratings. Moreover, we observed both alignments and contradictions among experts' opinions. By incorporating contextual assessment, our method demonstrated improved fairness in evaluating a driver and better recognition of their skills.

This paper addresses the challenge of unseen scene text instances during model training by leveraging a novel, efficient method called Zero-shot Optical Character Recognition. It's a straightforward approach that leverages pre-trained language models for unseen and seen text segments classification, thereby requiring minimal computational resources. Our experiment shows that it outperforms existing OCR models, including pre-trained vision-language ones, across various benchmarks.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of scientific disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, analysts have thoroughly examined Gaussian random fields, whereas more recent attention has been given to nonlinear system biology applications. This article serves as a comprehensive overview of applied random field statistics, focusing on spatial data, which includes a brief historical background, common challenges in data analysis, and commonly employed machine learning approaches. It also highlights a set of unresolved problems and proposes potential research directions, aiming to inspire the next generation of engineers, applied mathematicians, and machine learning specialists to work on interdisciplinary problems involving complex systems identified as "hard identified" in recent scientific literature.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $f$ that belongs to $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, we examine the standard $L$-function, denoted by $L(f,s)$, and its component $L^{(gl)}(f,s)$ that accounts for GL_2(\mathbb{Z})'s actions, focusing on the algebraic aspects. When the L-function's score s equals 11/2, a real part and 11/2, a conjugate part are provided, resulting in understanding of the denominators in algebraic part.
